Passing NULL as 'text' is an interface-contract question (documented GLFW behavior clears the clipboard), not attacker data.
The vulnerability requires a PLATFORM_WEB build; on a desktop-only build the defective sink is not compiled.

verdict.summary: qemu_register_machine consumes only internal, compile-time-defined QEMUMachine descriptors; m->name is a static literal, not data crossing a trust boundary. The missing NULL checks on m/m->name and the unchecked g_strconcat result are contract/robustness issues whose triggers require a caller contract violation or process-wide allocation failure on a fixed-size string — neither is attacker-instantiable, and the worst consequence is a crash of the registering process itself.

assumptions: This function is registered via QEMU's machine_init mechanism and invoked at startup with pointers to statically defined QEMUMachine structs; this code is not a parse/decode/protocol intake point.
g_strconcat returns NULL only on allocation failure; the concatenated string is a short compiled-in literal plus the constant TYPE_MACHINE_SUFFIX, so its size is fixed and not attacker-influenced.
limitations: No NULL check on parameter m or on m->name before g_strconcat(m->name, ...) — a caller violating the documented contract (passing NULL or a machine without a name) would crash the registering process at startup; robustness issue only, trigger not attacker-instantiable.
The return of g_strconcat is not checked before use as ti.name in type_register(&ti); reachable only via allocation failure on a fixed-size constant-size string, which no attacker can induce.

verdict.summary: In nfs3svc_decode_writeargs, the received-data validation guard 'if (dlen < XDR_QUADLEN(len)*4) return 0;' wraps for len in {0xFFFFFFFD, 0xFFFFFFFE, 0xFFFFFFFF} because XDR_QUADLEN computes ((len+3)>>2) in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic, so len+3 overflows to 0..2 and the guard reduces to 'dlen < 0' (always false). An NFS client can send a WRITE call with count == len == 0xFFFFFFFF and zero data bytes; the guard passes, then the clamp 'len = args->len = max_blocksize' sets the data length to the transport maximum while no data was received. The vec-filling loop then walks rq_pages[v]/rq_vec[v] with v derived only from the unvalidated len, mapping up to max_blocksize bytes of pages never filled by the request. Downstream, nfsd writes args->count bytes from these pages into the target file, persisting stale/uninitialized kernel memory (memory disclosure to the attacker-readable file), or dereferences an unpopulated page slot (remote kernel DoS).

evidence.reason: Defective guard: XDR_QUADLEN(len) = ((len+3)>>2) computed in unsigned 32-bit arithmetic wraps for len = 0xFFFFFFFD..0xFFFFFFFF, yielding 0, so the condition becomes 'dlen < 0' and accepts a WRITE whose declared length is ~2^32 with zero actually received data bytes (dlen can be 0). This is the only length-vs-received-data check in the function.

After the bypassed guard, the clamp sets len = args->count = max_blocksize without re-validating against dlen, so len (and the downstream write size) is raised to the transport maximum even though the attacker supplied no data bytes.

Sink: the loop bounds v solely by the unvalidated len, claiming a full PAGE_SIZE per rq_pages[v] for pages that were never filled by the request; the resulting rq_vec entries are consumed by nfsd3_proc_write to copy args->count bytes into the target file, reading stale/uninitialized kernel page contents (out-of-bounds read with disclosure) or dereferencing an unpopulated page slot.

Origin of the tainted value: len and args->len are read verbatim from the attacker-supplied XDR stream as a 32-bit unsigned value with no range restriction at intake; the attacker sets len = args->count = 0xFFFFFFFF to trigger the wrap at line 39.

assumptions: XDR_QUADLEN is taken as its kernel definition ((l)+3)>>2 evaluated in the operand's 32-bit unsigned type; the wrap analysis depends on this macro definition, which is external to the given code.

The value of svc_max_payload(rqstp) (transport-dependent, typically tens of KB to 1 MB) and the size/population policy of rq_pages[]/rq_vec[] (svc_alloc_arg, RPCSVC_MAXPAGES) are external to this code; the in-code defect is the missing validation of len against received data, whose only enforcement is the wrapping line 39.
decode_fh and xdr_decode_hyper consume only in-head words and are assumed not to move p outside head for well-formed calls; line 17 still re-checks p against the head end.
limitations: Whether the out-of-bounds page access manifests as a NULL dereference (page slot never populated for the message) or as disclosure of stale page contents depends on the sunrpc page-allocation policy, which is not shown; both consequences cross the network trust boundary (remote DoS or kernel memory disclosure into the attacker's file).

Exceeding the rq_vec[]/rq_pages[] array extents themselves (v beyond RPCSVC_MAXPAGES) is not provable from the given code since max_blocksize is set externally; the confirmed defect is the length-bypass and the resulting read of data-less pages.
args->offset is a full 64-bit attacker value; any overflow handling of it occurs downstream (not in this code) and was not analyzed.

Guard at line 17 uses '>' rather than '>=' (p == head end allowed), which yields a zero-length head vector; this is benign because dlen then counts only pages/tail and the line 39 check (when not wrapped) still bounds len.

verdict.summary: trim_spaces lacks a 'len > 0' bound: when the user-supplied string is empty or consists entirely of spaces, the loop index 'len - 1' underflows to -1, reading str[-1] out of bounds, and if that byte equals ' ' it writes '\0' to str[-1] and continues scanning/writing backward through heap memory before the buffer (memory corruption). The trigger is fully instantiated by argv[1] = "" or an all-space argument copied into buf2 and passed to trim_spaces.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the loop's only condition is str[len - 1] == ' ' with no check that len > 0. For an empty string (len = 0 from 'int len = strlen(str)') or an all-space string, len reaches 0 after 'len--' iterations and the condition evaluates str[-1]: an out-of-bounds read before the heap buffer, followed by an out-of-bounds write str[-1] = '\0' if that byte is ' ', corrupting heap metadata and continuing backward. Simulated trigger: argv[1] = "  " → strcpy into buf2 → trim_spaces(buf2) runs len 2→1→0, then reads/writes str[-1].

Taint origin: attacker-controlled argv[1] (empty or all-spaces string within the program's documented input surface) is copied into the heap buffer buf2 of size strlen(argv[1]) + 1 and passed to trim_spaces at line 34, delivering the value that underflows the loop index.

assumptions: malloc calls at lines 25-27 are assumed to succeed when reasoning about the trigger path; failure is environmental and not attacker-inducible.

The exact byte preceding buf2 is allocator-dependent; on glibc the chunk-size LSB is typically not 0x20, so the common outcome is the guaranteed out-of-bounds read at str[-1], with the out-of-bounds write arising under other heap layouts.
limitations: int len = strlen(str) truncates size_t to int, but argv strings are bounded well below INT_MAX by OS ARG_MAX limits, so the truncation is not triggerable through this program's input surface.
Unchecked malloc return values (lines 25-27) could yield NULL dereference, but only under allocation failure no attacker can induce.
buf1 and buf3 are allocated and freed unused; wasteful but not a security defect.
The out-of-bounds read value at str[-1] is only compared against ' ' and never printed, so there is no direct information disclosure from the read itself.

verdict.summary: qemu_register_machine is a startup-time registration shim that only consumes statically compiled QEMUMachine descriptors (m->name plus fixed constants). No attacker-influenced data crosses a trust boundary into this function, no memory/index/copy/injection/crypto/authz sink processes external content, and every candidate defect (unchecked m->name NULL, unchecked type_register result, unchecked g_strconcat allocation) requires a caller violating its compile-time contract, making it a robustness concern rather than a security vulnerability in this code.

assumptions: machine_class_init (not shown) casts class_data back to QEMUMachine* as designed; this code cannot be evaluated for that pair and no defect is observable here.
QEMU's machine descriptor tables that call this registration shim are statically compiled, so m and m->name originate inside the trusted process image, not from an external party.
g_strconcat aborts on allocation failure per glib defaults; the unchecked allocation result at line 3 is assumed not to silently return NULL under normal glib behavior.
limitations: Contract robustness: m and m->name are used without NULL checks (g_strconcat(m->name, ...) at line 3); a NULL machine descriptor or NULL name would crash QEMU during its own startup, but only the operator's own compiled code can produce that state, so it is not attacker-reachable and is a robustness bug, not a security vulnerability.

The return value of type_register(&ti) is ignored; a failed registration (e.g., duplicate type name) would silently skip a machine without propagating an error, a fail-silent robustness issue with no attacker-reachable trigger given static name tables.
ti.name (heap string from g_strconcat) is never freed, a bounded, startup-time-only leak of a few bytes per machine registration with no security impact.

verdict.summary: parse_mb_skip validates only 1 bit per row/column (`if (get_bits_left(&s->gb) < 1)`) in the SKIP_TYPE_ROW and SKIP_TYPE_COL paths, but the else branches then consume s->mb_width (resp. s->mb_height) bits per iteration via get_bits1 with no further availability check, unlike the SKIP_TYPE_MPEG case which verifies the full `s->mb_height * s->mb_width` bit count up front. A truncated WMV2 frame selecting these skip types drives the bitstream reader past the end of the attacker-supplied buffer (out-of-bounds read whose values flow into mb_type and the decode).

evidence.reason: Sink: SKIP_TYPE_ROW else branch consumes s->mb_width bits per row via get_bits1, while the only guard on the path (line 24, `if (get_bits_left(&s->gb) < 1)`) validates a single bit. Instantiated trigger: skip_type=2 from line 6, flag bit at line 26 reads 0, remaining bits = 0 after the flag — the loop still executes mb_width get_bits1 calls past the end of the bitstream buffer (out-of-bounds read).

Symmetric defect in SKIP_TYPE_COL: the else branch consumes s->mb_height bits per column while the only guard (line 39, `if (get_bits_left(&s->gb) < 1)`) covers one bit; a truncated stream with skip_type=3 and a 0 flag bit drives mb_height reads past the buffer end.
Origin of the tainted selector: the 2-bit skip_type is read from the attacker-controlled bitstream and dispatches into the defective SKIP_TYPE_ROW (2) / SKIP_TYPE_COL (3) paths.

assumptions: The mb_type array is assumed to be allocated with s->mb_stride columns covering mb_width and rows covering mb_height by the decoder's picture-allocation code (not shown); the write indices `mb_y * s->mb_stride + mb_x` could not be bounds-verified against the allocation inside this code.

The behavior of get_bits1/get_bits when the reader index passes the end of the buffer is implemented in the bitstream reader (not shown); no clamping or padding guarantee can be quoted from the given code, so the overreads are treated as reaching past the end of the input buffer.
SKIP_TYPE_NONE/MPEG/ROW/COL are assumed to enumerate all values 0..3 of the 2-bit skip_type, so the switch has no unhandled value.
limitations: Line 15 `if (get_bits_left(&s->gb) < s->mb_height * s->mb_width)`: the signed product could overflow int for extreme macroblock dimensions (~46341x46341), making the guard pass with too few bits; however no statement in this code can instantiate such dimensions and allocation of matching pictures elsewhere is presumed to fail first, so this is speculative.
Line 6 `get_bits(&s->gb, 2)` itself is not preceded by a bits-left check; it is the same missing-validation class as the primary finding but with a fixed 2-bit magnitude and is subsumed by it.
The 2-bit get_bits at line 6 with an empty bitstream would overread by at most 2 bits; treated as part of the same intake-validation defect rather than a separate finding.

verdict.summary: dbcs_ptr2len reads p[0] via MB_BYTE2LEN(*p) and conditionally reads p[1] only when the first byte is a DBCS lead byte (len == 2), which implies *p != NUL. For any in-contract NUL-terminated string, the terminator must occupy p[1] or a later byte, so the p[1] read is always in-bounds; the truncation case (lead byte immediately before NUL) is explicitly handled by 'if (len == 2 && p[1] == NUL) len = 1;'. The only hazardous scenario — a one-byte out-of-bounds read of p[1] — requires a caller to pass a buffer that is not NUL-terminated at or after p (e.g., a length-delimited field ending on a lead byte), which is a violation of the function's documented string contract and cannot be produced by any statement in this code (the function takes no length and performs no allocation or parsing). That scenario is therefore a contract/robustness limitation of the caller, not a vulnerability in this code.

assumptions: p is assumed to point to a NUL-terminated string, per the function's contract as Vim's DBCS pointer-length routine (its own 'p[1] == NUL' truncation check presupposes termination); Vim provides the separate dbcs_ptr2len_len for length-delimited buffers.
MB_BYTE2LEN(0) == 1 is assumed per Vim's DBCS byte-length tables, so *p == NUL never causes the p[1] read; this table is defined outside the given code.
char_u is Vim's unsigned char typedef, so *p is 0-255 with no sign-extension issue.
limitations: Contract-dependent one-byte out-of-bounds read: if a caller passes a non-NUL-terminated buffer whose final byte is a DBCS lead byte, 'if (len == 2 && p[1] == NUL)' reads one byte past the allocation. The trigger precondition (missing terminator inside the allocation) cannot be instantiated by this code's own statements and requires a caller contract violation, so it is recorded here rather than as a vulnerability; callers with length-delimited data must use a length-aware variant.
NULL-pointer dereference if p == NULL — interface contract question, not attack data; no check exists in this code but none is possible for a documented non-NULL string pointer.

verdict.summary: All attacker-influenced (file-derived) values reaching memory sinks in this Mach-O chained-fixup iterator are guarded inside this code: segment/chained_starts indexing is bounded by 'i < bin->nsegs && i < bin->segs_count', the page_start[] access is preceded by 'if (page_idx >= bin->chained_starts[i]->page_count) { break; }', page_size is sanitized via 'if (page_size < 1) { page_size = 4096; }', and the cursor walk is bounded by 'cursor < limit_end && cursor < end' plus the short-read break 'if (r_buf_read_at (bin->b, cursor, tmp, 8) != 8)'. The remaining arithmetic quirks (ut64 wrap of start+filesize, unsigned underflow of limit_end-8, page_size fallback) do not reach any memory, index, injection, or amplification sink. No trigger with material security impact could be instantiated.

assumptions: r_buf_read_at (RBuffer) clamps reads to the buffer extent and returns the number of bytes actually read, so a read at a wrapped or out-of-file cursor returns < 8 and triggers the quoted break — this is a library contract not visible in the given code.

The page_start[] flexible array inside dyld_chained_starts_in_segment is allocated with page_count entries by the parse code (not shown); the in-code guard 'page_idx >= bin->chained_starts[i]->page_count' enforces the intended bound but the allocation-size relationship itself is external to this snippet.
bin->segs has at least segs_count entries and bin->chained_starts has at least nsegs entries as maintained by the parse layer (not shown); the loop condition quotes both bounds.
bin is non-NULL and callback/context are supplied by a same-privilege caller (interface contract).
limitations: Unsigned underflow of 'limit_end - 8' when a caller passes limit_end in [1,7] makes the window filter fail open, so the callback can fire for a cursor whose 8-byte read extends past limit_end. The 8 bytes are still read successfully from the in-bounds buffer, and the callback is the caller's own code, so no memory, disclosure, injection, or amplification consequence exists; trigger also requires a contract-violating range from the caller.

'ut64 end = start + bin->segs[i].filesize' can wrap for attacker-chosen fileoff/filesize, but the wrapped value only tightens or bounds loop conditions; every actual read is gated by the short-read break, so no out-of-bounds access results.

A page_start value with the 0x8000 overflow-page encoding is treated as a plain offset (misinterpretation of the dyld format), which can make the cursor land outside the intended page; cursor remains bounded by 'cursor < end' and the read-length check, so this is a correctness issue, not memory unsafety.

'if (page_size < 1) { page_size = 4096; }' substitutes a default page size that may not match the file's real layout, mis-indexing page_start entries; all indices remain below page_count, so this is a logic inaccuracy only.

The rebasing_buffer flag toggling around r_buf_read_at is not reentrancy-safe if the callback re-enters the parser; the callback is a same-privilege contract argument, so this is a robustness concern.

verdict.summary: In split(), the second realloc-failure path calls free(copy) at line 29 after free(copy) at line 20 already released it — a double free (heap corruption) reachable whenever the final realloc fails, which an attacker can force because the function's memory consumption is driven by the unbounded attacker-supplied string 'arg' with no size bound in the code. Additionally, the guard 'if (!tmp && result)' (line 8) omits the first-iteration case where result==NULL, so a failed first realloc leads to 'result[i++] = dupstr(cptr)' writing through a NULL pointer (line 17).

evidence.reason: Double free (CWE-415): on the second realloc-failure path, 'copy' is freed here after line 20 ('free(copy);') already freed it; no statement between lines 20 and 29 re-arms or re-validates 'copy'. Trigger: attacker supplies a token-rich 'arg' whose unbounded duplication exhausts memory, the final realloc (line 23) returns NULL, the error path runs, and this second free corrupts the heap / aborts the process handling attacker data.

Origin of the same dangling pointer on the same execution path: this first free executes unconditionally before the 'if (i)' block, so the later free(copy) at line 29 on the error path is guaranteed to be a double free.

NULL-pointer write (CWE-476): the only failure guard, 'if (!tmp && result) {' (line 8), is false when the first realloc fails (tmp==NULL and result==NULL), so control falls through to 'result = tmp' (NULL) and 'result[0]' is written through a NULL pointer. Trigger instantiated by attacker-induced memory exhaustion at the first token; the process crashes handling attacker data.

assumptions: dupstr() is not shown; its semantics (duplicating strlen(arg)+1 bytes, possible NULL return on failure) are assumed and could add further unchecked-NULL issues (line 2 and line 17) not provable from the given code.
No caller is visible; per the intake-point rule, 'arg' is treated as attacker-supplied content and no external size limit is assumed (none is quotable in this code).
realloc failure is treated as attacker-inducible via memory exhaustion because this code's allocations scale with the unbounded attacker-controlled input and no in-code bound exists.
limitations: Integer overflow of 'i + 1' (lines 7/23) requires i==INT_MAX, i.e. ~2^31 tokens and ~16 GiB of successful prior reallocs; realloc would fail first, so this trigger is speculative.
If i==0 (empty string or all delimiters), the function returns NULL rather than an empty NULL-terminated array — a caller-contract ambiguity, not a memory-safety defect in this code.
The unchecked dupstr(cptr) at line 17 may store NULL mid-array if dupstr can fail, truncating consumer iteration — dependent on the unseen helper.

In a single-user CLI deployment where the same user supplies 'arg' at equal privilege and no service boundary is crossed, the worst-case crash of that process would be a robustness issue rather than a vulnerability; the verdict assumes a cross-boundary deployment (service parsing attacker data).

verdict.summary: dbcs_ptr2len reads only *p and p[1]. Given the documented contract that p points into a NUL-terminated (or buffer-backed) string, *p != NUL implies p[1] is readable (worst case it is the terminator byte), and MB_BYTE2LEN's 256-entry table is total over all byte values. No guard, arithmetic, or sink in this code can produce an out-of-bounds access from the data it consumes.

assumptions: MB_BYTE2LEN is defined (outside this snippet) as a lookup table of 256 entries covering all unsigned char values, so MB_BYTE2LEN(*p) is total and cannot index out of range.
The documented calling contract is that p points into a NUL-terminated string (Vim's ptr2len family of helpers); under that contract p[1] is always readable when *p != NUL.
limitations: Speculative CWE-125: if a caller passed a pointer to a lone DBCS lead byte at the end of a buffer with no NUL terminator, the read p[1] would be one byte out of bounds. This requires a caller contract violation (non-terminated buffer) not producible by this code's own flow, so it is not a vulnerability of this code.

verdict.summary: display_dollar() uses its colnr_T parameter 'col' as a byte offset into the current line buffer without any bound check: it computes 'p + col' on the pointer returned by ml_get_curline() and passes it to mb_head_off(), which dereferences bytes at/around that address. Nothing in the function verifies that col is within the current line's byte length (or non-negative), so any column value exceeding the (attacker-influenced) line length causes a heap out-of-bounds read at line 17.

evidence.reason: Unguarded out-of-bounds read (CWE-125): the index parameter 'col' (no validation anywhere in the function against the line length) is used as a byte offset, and mb_head_off() dereferences p + col. Trigger instantiated: col = 5 with current line "a" (L = 1) makes p + col point 4 bytes past the NUL terminator; mb_head_off reads heap memory outside the line buffer.

Origin of the tainted index: the colnr_T parameter 'col' is the sole data-carrying input of this intake point; it flows unmodified into the pointer arithmetic 'p + col' at line 17 with no intervening bound check.

assumptions: colnr_T is a signed long (Vim's declaration), so 'col' may also be negative, making p + col read before the buffer; no sign check exists in this code.
mb_head_off(base, p2) dereferences bytes at p2 and walks backward while they look like multibyte continuation bytes; its contract is quoted from the codebase, not shown here.
ml_get_curline() returns the NUL-terminated current line whose byte length is determined by the edited buffer content (attacker-influenced).
The callers of display_dollar are not shown; per the analysis rules the parameter is treated as attacker-data at this intake point rather than deferring validation to the callers.
limitations: The effect of the out-of-range w_cursor.col inside curs_columns(FALSE) (line 19) cannot be evaluated within this snippet; it is treated as a consequence of the confirmed over-read, not a separate finding.

A signed-underflow of w_cursor.col at line 17 (mb_head_off returning more than col) is not independently instantiable while p + col is in bounds; it only occurs once the primary over-read has already happened.
If every possible caller in the full program could be proven to pass only in-bounds byte columns, the practical exploitability would drop, but no such guarantee is quotable from the given code.

verdict.summary: All memory-access sinks in iterate_chained_fixups are guarded by quotable in-code checks (segment index bound by 'i < bin->nsegs && i < bin->segs_count', page index bound by 'page_idx >= ...->page_count' plus a NULL check on page_start, and buffer reads validated by 'r_buf_read_at(...) != 8'), all locals (delta, stride, addend, carry_on, key, addr_div, diversity, ptr_value) are initialized on every consuming path, and loops make strict positive progress with bounds derived from the file's own real size. Remaining concerns (ut64 wrap of end=start+filesize, limit_end-8 underflow for sub-8 limits, USERLAND24 using non-24-bit struct layouts, and parse-site allocation sizes) either cannot be instantiated from this code's input surface or have no memory-safety or boundary-crossing consequence.

assumptions: bin->segs, bin->chained_starts, and chained_starts->page_start arrays are allocated at the parse site (not shown) with sizes consistent with nsegs, segs_count, and page_count respectively; the in-code index guards quote those counts as bounds.
r_buf_read_at performs bounds-safe reads at any offset and returns the number of bytes read; the code checks 'r_buf_read_at (bin->b, cursor, tmp, 8) != 8' before using tmp.
The dyld_chained_ptr_* bitfield structs total at most 64 bits, so casting &raw_ptr (an 8-byte local) to them is memory-safe.
RFixup{Bind,BindAuth,Rebase,RebaseAuth}EventDetails structs have no members beyond those explicitly assigned before each callback invocation.
limit_start/limit_end/event_mask/callback/context are framework-internal interface-contract arguments, not file-derived attacker content.
limitations: ut64 overflow in 'ut64 end = start + bin->segs[i].filesize;' can wrap end below start, causing (R_MIN(limit_end,end)-start) to underflow into a huge page_end_idx; the page loop is still capped at page_count iterations by 'if (page_idx >= bin->chained_starts[i]->page_count) break;' and no out-of-range access results — robustness-only.
'cursor <= limit_end - 8' underflows if the caller passes limit_end < 8; not attacker-reachable (contract argument) and cursor remains constrained by 'cursor < limit_end'.

The DYLD_CHAINED_PTR_ARM64E_USERLAND24 case interprets rebase/auth-rebase values through the non-24-bit arm64e struct layouts, producing semantically wrong fixup fields; memory-safe (reads bitfields of the 8-byte local raw_ptr) — correctness bug only.

Speculative: an out-of-bounds read of page_start[page_idx] would require the parse site (not shown) to allocate fewer than page_count entries; this code's own guard 'if (page_idx >= bin->chained_starts[i]->page_count) break;' is present on every path.
Speculative: the callback could misuse attacker-controlled 'ordinal' (bind ordinal from file) to index import tables without validation in callback code not shown; not provable in this code.
While-loop cost is linear in the real file size (reads fail past the buffer, breaking the loop); no attacker-scalable amplification found.

verdict.summary: ff_h264_pred_weight_table uses the attacker-controlled slice-header value ref_count[list] as the loop bound (line 27) with no bounds check anywhere in the function, then writes through indices i and 16+2*i into the fixed-size arrays pwt->luma_weight[32][2][2] and pwt->chroma_weight[32][2][2][2]. For a frame picture (picture_structure == PICT_FRAME) with ref_count >= 9 (spec-legal up to 32), the duplication write at 16+2*i reaches index >= 32, an out-of-bounds write of attacker-influenced int values into the decoder's memory when parsing a malicious H.264 stream.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted index: ref_count[list] is derived from the attacker-controlled num_ref_idx_active slice-header field and directly becomes the loop bound for i. No statement in this function validates ref_count[list] against the 32-entry array dimension or the 8-entry limit required by the frame-duplication index 16+2*i, so this code's own loop produces the out-of-range index.

Out-of-bounds write sink. Instantiated trigger: attacker stream with picture_structure == PICT_FRAME and ref_count[0] = 16 (num_ref_idx_active_minus1 = 15, spec-legal). At i = 8 the loop reaches these statements and writes pwt->luma_weight[16 + 2*8 = 32][list][*] — index 32 of the [32][2][2] array — storing attacker-influenced int values (luma_def or an attacker se(v) weight in [-128,127]); i up to 31 (ref_count up to 32) reaches index 79, spilling into chroma_weight, implicit_weight, and beyond the struct. No index bound exists on any path to this sink.

assumptions: H264PredWeightTable::luma_weight is declared [32][2][2] and chroma_weight [32][2][2][2] (the struct definition is outside the given code; taken as type information, not as a runtime guard).

ref_count[] values derive from the H.264 slice header's num_ref_idx_active, parsed outside this function; per guard-anchoring, any caller-side bound on ref_count is an assumption and cannot be treated as a defense provided by this code.
PICT_FRAME, AV_PICTURE_TYPE_B, and num_ref_idx_active up to 32 are normal, attacker-selectable decode states within the H.264 input surface, not contract violations.
limitations: If the (unshown) caller clamped ref_count[list] to <= 8 for frame pictures, the frame-duplication overflow would be unreachable; no such check exists in this code, and even spec-maximum ref_count = 32 triggers indices up to 79.
Behavior of get_ue_golomb/get_se_golomb on exhausted bitstreams (e.g., returning filler values) is defined by the bit reader outside this code and was not evaluated.

The range checks on luma/chroma_log2_weight_denom (lines 11, 18) and on se(v) weights (lines 33-35, 52-54) were edge-tested (0, 7, 8, -1, 127, 128, -129, negative-after-unsigned-store) and found sound; they bound content but not the array index, so they do not mitigate the primary finding.

verdict.summary: sanity_check_ckpt accumulates five attacker-controlled u32 on-disk segment counts into the unsigned int fsmeta (lines 9-13) with no overflow check; a crafted superblock/checkpoint whose component sum exceeds UINT32_MAX (e.g. segment_count_ckpt=0xFFFFFFFF plus small components) wraps fsmeta to a small value, bypassing both the 'fsmeta >= total' check (line 15) and the F2FS_MIN_SEGMENTS check (line 21), so a grossly invalid filesystem layout passes this kernel intake validation gate (return 0) and the wrapped metadata count drives downstream kernel mount/sizing logic.

evidence.reason: Root cause: unchecked unsigned 32-bit overflow in the fsmeta accumulation of five attacker-supplied le32 on-disk values. Instantiated trigger: total=16, segment_count_ckpt=0xFFFFFFFF, segment_count_sit=2, segment_count_nat=2, ckpt->rsvd_segment_count=2, segment_count_ssa=3 -> fsmeta wraps to 8 (true sum 4294967308), so the line-15 guard 'fsmeta >= total' (8 >= 16 = false) and the line-21 'fsmeta < F2FS_MIN_SEGMENTS' guard are both bypassed and the function returns 0, accepting an invalid layout at the kernel's trust boundary for untrusted filesystem images.

assumptions: raw_super and ckpt fields originate from an on-disk f2fs image (superblock/checkpoint) whose contents are attacker-controlled when an untrusted user mounts a crafted image; all values are le32 (32-bit) as consumed via le32_to_cpu.

F2FS_MIN_SEGMENTS is a small compile-time constant (on the order of 6), so a wrapped fsmeta of 8 satisfies 'fsmeta >= F2FS_MIN_SEGMENTS'; the attacker can tune the wrap target to any value including ones above it.
f2fs_cp_error(sbi) is internal kernel state, false on a fresh mount, so it does not block the trigger.

Downstream consumers of fsmeta/total (mount-time array sizing and segment layout) are outside this code; the impact asserted here is the fail-open validation of attacker image data at this intake gate, with the wrapped value flowing onward after return 0.
limitations: ovp_segments and reserved_segments (lines 18-19) are validated only against 0 in this function and are not bounded by total here; their use as sizing values occurs in code not shown, so no in-function defect is claimed for them.

The precise downstream memory-corruption site (allocation/indexing based on the wrapped fsmeta) lies in code outside this function and was not analyzed; severity reflects the fail-open intake validation plus the wrap value's onward flow.

verdict.summary: my_strdup allocates strlen(str) bytes without room for the terminating NUL, then strcpy copies strlen(str)+1 bytes, writing one byte past the end of the heap allocation. Any non-NULL argument (e.g. argv[1] from main) instantiates a heap off-by-one out-of-bounds write with attacker-chosen length that can corrupt adjacent heap chunk metadata.

evidence.reason: Origin of the defect: the allocation is sized strlen(str) bytes, omitting the +1 needed for the string terminator; no statement anywhere in the code adds 1 or bounds the size.

Sink: strcpy writes strlen(str)+1 bytes (including the trailing NUL) into the strlen(str)-byte buffer from line 12, producing a one-byte heap out-of-bounds write. Trigger fully instantiated by main passing argv[1] (e.g. "AB": malloc(2), strcpy writes 3 bytes); the only guards present are NULL checks that do not affect the size mismatch.

assumptions: main's argv[1] is treated as attacker-originated content (untrusted input crossing the process boundary), so my_strdup must be the last line of defense for the string it duplicates.
malloc(0) behavior is implementation-defined; on implementations returning a non-NULL unique pointer, an empty-string argument still produces a 1-byte OOB write.
limitations: printf("%s", copy) at line 30 receives NULL if malloc fails (my_strdup returns NULL); this requires an allocation failure of a tiny size, is not attacker-inducible, and at worst is a crash/UB of the equal-privilege process — robustness issue, not a vulnerability.

The attacker model here is a user supplying a command-line argument to a process they themselves run; the finding stands because memory corruption (1-byte NUL overwrite past an attacker-length-controlled heap chunk, capable of corrupting adjacent chunk metadata) is never demoted to robustness.

verdict.summary: No fully instantiated security vulnerability found. The 'CC +' path's allocation `malloc(strlen(comment)+strlen(newcomment)+2)` is exactly sufficient because `r_str_unescape` cannot lengthen `nc`; format strings are literals; all indexed reads of `input` are NUL-terminated-safe. Remaining issues (unchecked strdup/malloc NULL derefs, command-string construction in undo records) are robustness concerns whose triggers are allocation failure or replay code not present here.

assumptions: `r_meta_set_string`, `r_str_newf`, `sdb_decode`, `r_num_math`, and `getcommapath` behave per their contracts (valid lengths, NUL termination) — their implementations are not shown.
The `input` string is NUL-terminated; reading `input[1]`, `input[2]` past a short string stops at the terminator (case 0) and later index reads occur only on paths where earlier bytes are non-NUL.
Undo-record strings built via `r_str_newf("CC %s@0x%08"PFMT64x, nc, addr)` are consumed by replay logic outside this snippet.
limitations: Unchecked `strdup`/`malloc` results (`nc = strdup(newcomment)`, `s = strdup(s+1)`) could be NULL and dereferenced by `r_str_unescape`/`strchr` on allocation failure — environment-triggered crash only, not attacker-inducible.

Comment text `nc` is embedded unescaped into an undo command string ("CC %s@...") which, if replayed as an r2 command by undo logic (not shown), could allow command injection via characters like '@' or ';' — trigger precondition (replay semantics and operator invoking undo on own input) cannot be instantiated in this code.
Worst-case outcomes for malformed user commands (e.g., empty usage errors, `r_num_math` on garbage) are confined to the operator's own process.

verdict.summary: The libc-replacement calloc correctly guards the n*lb multiplication against size_t overflow with 'if (lb && n > SIZE_MAX / lb) return NULL;' placed on every path before both allocation sites (GC_malloc_uncollectable(n*lb) and REDIRECT_MALLOC(n*lb)). Edge testing at lb==0, n==0, n==SIZE_MAX/lb exactly, and one-past-limit shows the guard rejects all overflowing products; no other memory, injection, crypto, or authz sink exists in this code.

assumptions: REDIRECT_MALLOC, GC_malloc_uncollectable, and GC_init_lib_bounds are external callees not shown; their internal behavior (e.g., whether GC_malloc_uncollectable itself validates its size argument) is assumed per their contract, not verified here.

GC_init_lib_bounds() is assumed to set GC_libpthread_start/end and GC_libld_start/end to coherent values; if it leaves them at 0, the range comparisons at lines 18-21 simply fail, which has no security effect since caller is never dereferenced.
GC_malloc_uncollectable/REDIRECT_MALLOC are assumed to return NULL on allocation failure per the documented calloc contract; this code propagates that NULL, which is correct libc behavior.
limitations: The static flag 'lib_bounds_set' (line 10) is not synchronized; a data race could cause GC_init_lib_bounds() to run more than once or a thread to briefly use bounds from a prior initialization. No memory-unsafe or attacker-controllable consequence is instantiated by any statement in this code; treated as a robustness concern.

The return address of the caller is compared against library ranges as a heuristic to decide collectability; a caller whose return address spuriously falls in the libpthread range would receive an uncollectable allocation. This is a memory-retention heuristic, not a reachable memory-safety defect, and the address is compared, never dereferenced.
If the platform size_t were narrower than the product the caller intends, the guard correctly returns NULL rather than wrapping; no truncation occurs because n and lb are never cast before use.

verdict.summary: ff_h264_pred_weight_table uses the attacker-derived, uncapped ref_count[list] parameter as the only bound on loop index i (line 26) while writing fixed-size arrays pwt->luma_weight[i][list][*] and, when picture_structure == PICT_FRAME, the doubled entries pwt->luma_weight[16+2*i][list][*] and pwt->chroma_weight[16+2*i][list][j][*]. No statement in this code bounds ref_count, so a slice header yielding ref_count = 17 (or more) makes the loop write at array index 16+2*16 = 48 and beyond — an out-of-bounds write of attacker-influenced integers in the decoder processing a malicious H.264 stream.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink: with ref_count[list] = 17 (attacker-set via num_ref_idx_active in the slice header) and picture_structure == PICT_FRAME, i reaches 16 and these statements write fixed-size member arrays at first-dimension index 16+2*16 = 48 and 16+2*16+1 = 49 (and chroma_weight at the same indices), past the array capacity the 16+2*i fan-out was designed for (i <= 15, max index 47); the writes carry attacker-influenced golomb weights or luma_def/chroma_def. No bound on ref_count exists anywhere in this function.

Origin of the tainted index: the loop bound is the attacker-derived parameter ref_count[list] (parsed from the untrusted bitstream upstream), which is never compared against, clamped, or otherwise bounded by any statement in this code; it is the sole limit on i for every luma_weight[i]/chroma_weight[i] and doubled-index write, so any value above the array capacity (17 for frame pictures, or above the raw table size) produces out-of-bounds writes.

assumptions: The dimensions of H264PredWeightTable are not shown in the given code; the known FFmpeg definition uses luma_weight[48][2][2] and chroma_weight[48][2][2][2], consistent with the 16+2*i fan-out design (max index 47 for i<=15). The finding does not depend on the exact size: ref_count is uncapped, so some finite attacker-chosen value exceeds any fixed array dimension.
gb, sps, ref_count, slice_type_nos and picture_structure are assumed to carry attacker-chosen content from the encoded H.264 stream, per the decoder trust boundary.
gb, sps, pwt, logctx are assumed non-NULL per the internal interface contract (contract arguments, not attack data).
limitations: pwt->chroma_log2_weight_denom is read at line 17 without having been assigned when sps->chroma_format_idc == 0 (assignment at line 12 is conditional), and lines 73-74 copy chroma_weight[i][list][j] entries that were never written in that case — a potential CWE-457/CWE-908 uninitialized-value issue. The >7U check bounds any surviving value to [0,7] so no UB shift occurs, and the impact is limited to wrong prediction weights; whether the containing struct is actually uninitialized depends on allocation code not shown, so this is recorded here rather than as a primary finding.
get_se_golomb weight magnitudes are correctly range-checked by the (int8_t) round-trip comparisons at lines 32-34 and 51-53, which fail closed via out_range_weight; no candidate survived there.
luma_log2_weight_denom / chroma_log2_weight_denom shift amounts are correctly bounded to [0,7] by the > 7U checks (lines 13 and 17), which also neutralize negative values via unsigned conversion.

verdict.summary: op_format manipulates only internal, same-privilege editor state (cursor positions, marks, line-count deltas) supplied by the operator machinery of the user's own editor session. The one memory-adjacent increment is correctly guarded by 'curwin->w_cursor.lnum < curbuf->b_ml.ml_line_count', and the u_save result is checked for FAIL with an early return. The unvalidated oap->cursor_start and the unclamped w_old_*_lnum adjustment can only be shown harmful via code not present here (caller initialization, redraw consumers), and the realistic worst case is a crash of the equal-privilege editing process itself, which is a robustness issue, not a security vulnerability.

assumptions: oap->cursor_start, oap->start, oap->end are initialized by the operator machinery (do_pending_operator, not shown) to valid in-buffer positions; this code contains no statement producing or validating them.
u_save (not shown) treats top == 0 as 'save from top' and handles bot beyond the last line; the call u_save(start.lnum-1, end.lnum+1) follows the canonical Vim idiom.
format_lines (not shown) leaves curwin->w_cursor on a valid line within the formatted region, and w_old_cursor_lnum/w_old_visual_lnum are only consumed by the not-shown redraw code.
cmdmod.cmod_flags and the CMOD_LOCKMARKS flag are set by Ex-command parsing before the operator runs.
limitations: Candidate A (speculative): 'curwin->w_cursor = oap->cursor_start;' assigns an unvalidated position; a cursor_start.lnum == 0 would propagate an invalid cursor into beginline/mark code. Trigger requires the caller to leave cursor_start unset, which this code neither produces nor checks; additionally the worst case is a crash of the user's own equal-privilege editor (robustness).

Candidate B (speculative): 'u_save((linenr_T)(oap->start.lnum - 1), (linenr_T)(oap->end.lnum + 1))' could underflow/overflow only at lnum 0 or lnum == LONG_MAX, neither of which any statement in this code can produce; also this call is guarded against failure by an explicit '== FAIL' early return.

Candidate C (in-code-instantiated but no in-code sink): in the FOR_ALL_WINDOWS loop, 'wp->w_old_cursor_lnum += old_line_count;' has only a '!= 0' pre-check; with a negative old_line_count (formatting that joins lines) the sum can become 0 or negative (e.g. 3 + (-12) = -9), breaking the redraw invariant. The value is only stored in this code; the consumers live in the redraw code that is not given, so no memory/index sink could be proven here, and the reachable worst case is mis-rendering or a crash of the same equal-privilege process.

verdict.summary: unix_getpw dereferences encrypted_pass at 'if (encrypted_pass[0] == 0)' without any NULL check. encrypted_pass is assigned from unchecked password-database lookup results ('encrypted_pass = pwd->pw_passwd;' and 'encrypted_pass = spwd->sp_pwdp;'), and the only NULL test in the function (line 59) guards strlen on the pre-shadow value only, is compiled out entirely when HAVE_GETSPNAM is undefined, and never re-checks the shadow value it substitutes. A remote RADIUS client controls the User-Name (line 27) and can select an account whose passwd/shadow password field is NULL — a condition the code's own guard and comment at lines 53-59 explicitly anticipate — causing a NULL dereference and crash (denial of service) of the shared authentication daemon.

evidence.reason: Unguarded dereference sink: encrypted_pass[0] is read with no NULL check on any path. encrypted_pass can be NULL here because it was assigned from getpwnam/getspnam lookup results without validation; trigger: a remote RADIUS client sends an Access-Request whose User-Name selects an account with a NULL password field, producing a NULL dereference and crashing the authentication daemon (network-triggered DoS).

Origin of the tainted value: the shadow-lookup result sp_pwdp is assigned to encrypted_pass with no NULL check; the preceding test at line 59 checked only the old passwd value, so a shadow entry with sp_pwdp == NULL propagates directly to the line-129 dereference.

Secondary origin: on builds without HAVE_GETSPNAM this unchecked getpwnam result is the only assignment of encrypted_pass, and no NULL check exists anywhere on the path from this line to the line-129 dereference.

assumptions: request->username->vp_strvalue is assumed NUL-terminated by the RADIUS decode layer (not shown in this code); no length bound on 'name' is enforced inside this function.

The semantics of a RLM_MODULE_NOOP return (candidate C4, passwordless account at line 130) are determined by the module caller, which is not shown; it cannot be established here as an authentication bypass.
pairmake/pairmove/pairfree behavior (lines 132-136) is external and assumed to operate on the possibly-non-NULL vp list per its contract; not attacker-controllable here.
limitations: OSFC2-only logic inversion at line 38 ('if (pr_pw->uflg.fg_lock!=1)' returns USERLOCK) is suspicious but Tru64/OSF pr_passwd flag semantics and the OSFC2 build could not be instantiated, so it is speculative.

pwd->pw_shell could theoretically be NULL at the strcmp sinks (lines 75, 88, 96), but no path in this code produces a NULL pw_shell and the standard files backend returns an empty string; not instantiated.

Secondary low-severity candidate (not ranked primary): the attacker-controlled User-Name 'name' is interpolated with %s into authentication logs at lines 39, 76-77, 95-96 with no sanitization, permitting log forging (CWE-117); the verdict and CWE are driven by the fully instantiated NULL-dereference DoS.
The strlen < 10 boundary at line 59 (exactly 10-character garbage treated as a crypt password) only causes a failed comparison and has no security effect.

verdict.summary: The strdup implementation is correctly guarded: str is NULL-checked, the heap buffer is allocated with the exact required size malloc(strlen(str) + 1), the allocation result is NULL-checked before strcpy, and main frees the copy exactly once and uses a fixed printf format. The only theoretical defects (size_t overflow at strlen(str)+1 requiring a 2^64-1-byte string, and a strlen/strcpy TOCTOU) cannot be instantiated by any input this program can receive, and the worst reachable outcome for the sole attacker (the user supplying argv[1] to their own unprivileged CLI) is a crash of their own process with nothing disclosed, written, or amplified.

assumptions: argv[1] is a NUL-terminated C string per the C standard's argv contract; the code's own strlen/strcpy usage depends on this, which is a documented interface contract of the C runtime, not an enforcement visible in the code.
malloc returns a suitably aligned block of the requested size on success, per the C standard library contract.
limitations: strlen(str) + 1 wraps only if the string length equals SIZE_MAX; no input surface of this program (argv strings) can supply such a string, so this overflow is speculative.

A TOCTOU between strlen (line 20) and strcpy (line 22) would require concurrent mutation of str; this code is single-threaded with no signal handlers or aliasing statements that can produce the race, so it is not instantiable here.

malloc is used in my_strdup (line 20) before #include <stdlib.h> appears (line 26) in the given source order; this is a declaration/compilation defect, not a runtime security issue reachable by an attacker.

If malloc fails or argv[1] is malformed, the process simply exits; the input supplier is the equal-privilege user running the CLI on their own arguments, so per the impact model this is robustness, not a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: write_refcount_block_entries computes the write size from first_index/last_index with no validation against the capacity of s->refcount_block_cache, and its own round-up 'last_index = (last_index + REFCOUNTS_PER_SECTOR) & ~(REFCOUNTS_PER_SECTOR - 1)' pushes last_index one sector past the buffer even for a fully in-range caller, so bdrv_pwrite reads out-of-bounds heap memory and writes it into the attacker-supplied qcow2 image (host memory disclosure), or faults the process (DoS).

evidence.reason: Sink: size bytes are read starting at &s->refcount_block_cache[first_index] with no bounds check anywhere in the function; when last_index is rounded past the cache end (see lines 9-11) this reads out of bounds and bdrv_pwrite writes the leaked heap contents into the qcow2 file the attacker can read. Simulated trigger: first_index=2047, last_index=2047 (valid, cache holds 2048 entries) -> line 8: first_index=1792; lines 9-10: last_index=2304; line 11: size=1024 -> reads entries 1792..2303, i.e. 512 bytes past the buffer.

Origin of the out-of-range value: the round-up of last_index adds a full sector of entries beyond the caller's index and size is computed from it without any comparison to the refcount_block_cache capacity, producing a size that over-reads the buffer at the sink on line 15; the minimal fixing guard (clamp/reject last_index against the cache capacity) is absent from every path in the given code.

assumptions: REFCOUNTS_PER_SECTOR and REFCOUNT_SHIFT macro values are not shown; assumed 256 and 1 (512-byte sector of 16-bit refcounts), both powers of two so the masks behave as alignment operations; the defect holds for any power-of-two values.

The allocation size of s->refcount_block_cache is not shown; assumed it holds one refcount block (e.g. 2048 entries for a 4096-byte cluster), used only to instantiate concrete numbers in the STEP 4 simulation.

The caller of this static function is not shown; per the rules its constraints cannot be used to dismiss the missing bound, and the trigger uses only indices valid at entry, defeated by this code's own round-up.
cache_refcount_updates is a global whose value is assumed enabled for the shown branch to execute.
The qcow2 image being modified is attacker-supplied and attacker-readable, so bytes written into it constitute cross-boundary disclosure.
limitations: Code is truncated after 'return ret;' (line 17); the non-caching path and success return are not analyzable.
Signed overflow of 'last_index + REFCOUNTS_PER_SECTOR' (line 9) at INT_MAX-scale values is speculative: no statement in this code produces values of that scale, and no quoted bound exists either way.
A negative first_index reaching the sink requires an unseen caller passing a negative index; recorded as part of the same missing-validation defect but not separately proven.
bs==NULL is an interface-contract question, not a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: decrypt_response parses the card's response header by reading in[0], in[2], in[3], and in[4] before any validation of inlen. A malicious smart card returning a short response body (e.g., inlen = 2) causes out-of-bounds reads past the valid response data; the only length check (cipher_len < 2 || i+cipher_len > inlen || cipher_len > sizeof plaintext) executes after these reads and does not bound the header indices.

evidence.reason: The parse cascade reads in[2] (line 20), in[3] (line 24), and in[4] (line 28) with no prior check that inlen >= 3/4/5. Trigger instantiated: card sends a 2-byte response {0x98, 0x7F} (inlen = 2); after the in[0] != 0x99 test at line 16, the condition `0x01 == in[2]` dereferences in[2] past the 2 valid bytes — an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) driven by the untrusted card response.

evidence.snippet: decrypt_response(struct sc_card *card, unsigned char *in, size_t inlen, unsigned char *out, size_t * out_len)
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted data: `in` (card response content) and `inlen` (card-controlled response length) cross the smart-card/host trust boundary at this entry point; they are consumed by the unguarded header reads at lines 16, 20, 24, and 28 before the length check at line 37.

assumptions: aes128_decrypt_cbc/des3_decrypt_cbc (not shown) are assumed to write at most their length argument (cipher_len - 1 <= 4095) into plaintext; their internal bounds cannot be verified here.
Only inlen bytes of `in` are documented valid; the actual allocation size of `in` in callers is not shown.
exdata (smtype, sk_enc) is driver-internal secure-messaging state treated as trusted.
limitations: memcpy(out, plaintext, cipher_len - 2) copies an attacker-influenced length (up to 4094 bytes) with no output-capacity parameter anywhere in the interface; an overflow of `out` could not be instantiated because the caller's buffer size is not shown — recorded as an interface/design concern, not a confirmed defect.
The 0x99 early-return path returns 0 without setting *out_len; any use of a stale/uninitialized *out_len lies in unseen caller code.

If callers pass a fixed-capacity buffer larger than the actual response (a common APDU pattern), reads of in[1..4] beyond inlen may land inside that allocation as uninitialized-data reads rather than object-level out-of-bounds accesses; the defect is out-of-bounds with respect to the documented valid length inlen.

verdict.summary: All writes in fp48_write_bin are bounded by exact-equality length guards quoted on every path ('if (len != 32 * RLC_FP_BYTES)' and 'if (len != 48 * RLC_FP_BYTES)'), each preceding the fixed-size component writes whose total footprint exactly matches the verified length, so no memory-safety defect exists. The only anomaly is a dead store: the pack branch computes fp48_pck(t, a) but serializes a's components instead of t's. Because fp48_pck is still invoked before the writes, its validation/exception behavior is preserved, and under RELIC's validate-and-copy packing semantics the output bytes are identical; any divergence would depend on unshown callee transform behavior, so no security consequence (memory, injection, authz, or crypto impact) is instantiable from the given code. The potential leak of t cannot be confirmed because the snippet is truncated before the function's RLC_FINALLY/free site.

assumptions: fp48_pck, fp8_write_bin, and fp24_write_bin contracts are not shown: it is assumed (not quotable) that the write helpers serialize exactly their len argument and that fp48_pck validates its input and produces the packed form, throwing on invalid elements (which would skip the writes at lines 14-17 since the call at line 13 precedes them).
The snippet is truncated mid-function (no RLC_CATCH_ANY, RLC_FINALLY, fp48_free(t), or closing brace); it is assumed the real function frees t and rethrows in the unshown remainder.
RLC_FP_BYTES is assumed to be a fixed positive compile-time constant and RLC_THROW a non-local exit, so the length guards abort the write paths.
No caller is shown; bin (non-NULL) is treated as an interface-contract argument, while len and a are treated as attacker-influenced data per STEP 1 and are validated in-function.
limitations: Lines 13-17: the packed form t produced by fp48_pck(t, a) is never read; the pack branch serializes a[0][1], a[0][2], a[1][0], a[1][2] instead of t's components. Under RELIC's pck pattern (validate then copy, e.g., 'fp6_copy(c[0][0], a[0][0]);' in fp12_pck) the output is byte-identical and the element-validity check still executes, so no security effect was instantiable; if fp48_pck transformed values in some unshown configuration, this would be a serialization-correctness deviation (wrong/non-canonical packed bytes), but that behavior cannot be quoted from the given code and no memory-safety sink is affected in either case.
Line 7 allocates t but no fp48_free(t) appears in the shown text; because the function body is visibly truncated, the leak trigger could not be instantiated and is speculative.
Passing bin == NULL or a == NULL would fault, but these are interface-contract arguments (documented non-NULL), not attack data per STEP 1.

verdict.summary: No exploitable vulnerability found. The only attacker-data input, the setting name (std::string), is used exclusively in exact-match or bounds-safe comparisons: the log sink is reachable only when name equals the constants 'mg_name'/'mg_flags' (guarding against log forging), and std::string::compare(0,7,...) clamps its count, so short/empty names are safe. The two apparent authorization relaxations (skipping the disallowed blocklist when getGuiEngine(L) is non-null, and allowing 'secure.' settings when isSecure(L) is false) are only reachable by the operator-privileged mainmenu environment or when the operator has deliberately disabled the mod sandbox — parties at equal privilege per the impact model — and the code's own statements cannot produce the mislabeled state that would be needed to instantiate a bypass.

assumptions: ScriptApiSecurity::isSecure(L) is assumed to correctly report the sandbox status of each Lua state; if a sandboxed state were mislabeled insecure, the 'secure.' guard on line 3 would fail open, but no statement in this code can produce that state.

ModApiBase::getGuiEngine(L) is assumed to return a non-null GUIEngine only for the mainmenu Lua state; if it returned non-null for a sandboxed (e.g., client-side mod) state, the blocklist on lines 21-26 would be skipped for untrusted code, but this code only propagates the callee's result (line 8) and cannot produce that condition.
The disallowed[] blocklist is assumed to be paired with equivalent checks wherever other dangerous settings are consumed; consumption sites are outside this snippet and were not verifiable here.
limitations: Mainmenu-state code can set every disallowed setting (blocklist gated on !is_mainmenu); this is by design so the mainmenu can configure serverlist_url/contentdb_url, and mainmenu scripts run at the operator's full privilege, so no cross-boundary impact was instantiable.

In environments where isSecure(L) is false, 'secure.' settings are settable; untrusted code does not run in such environments (sandbox deliberately disabled by the operator or trusted mainmenu), so no attacker at a lower privilege can reach this path.

The disallowed blocklist may not enumerate every security-sensitive setting (e.g., credential or font_path settings); exploiting an omitted name would require a sink outside this code, which could not be exhibited.

The values written to errorstream/infostream are attacker-influenced only if the line-10 equality guards could be passed with non-literal content; exact string equality makes that unreachable, so no CWE-117 log forging is possible via this function.

verdict.summary: html_escape's length-counting loop and copy loop use identical per-entity constants ('&'=5, '<'/'>'=4, '"'/'''=6, default=1), so the malloc(len+1) buffer is sized exactly and no out-of-bounds write occurs; all five HTML metacharacters (& < > " ') are escaped, preventing XSS when the message is rendered; get_welcome_message's total_length = strlen(prefix)+strlen(escaped)+strlen(suffix)+1 exactly matches the bytes written by strcpy/strcat including the final NUL (no off-by-one even for an empty username); all malloc results are NULL-checked and error paths free correctly with no double-free or leak. The only theoretical defect, size_t accumulation wrap in the len counter or in len+1, requires an input on the order of 2^64 bytes and cannot be instantiated; no guard exists for it, so it is recorded as a speculative limitation rather than a vulnerability.

assumptions: The rendering context of the welcome message is HTML text or a double-quoted attribute, as stated in the docstring ('rendered in a HTML page'); the escaped character set (& < > " ') is sufficient for those contexts.

No caller of get_welcome_message beyond main is shown; main is an unprivileged CLI where argv[1] is supplied by the user running the process at equal privilege, so crash-only outcomes from argv[1] are out of the attacker-impact model.
limitations: Speculative: size_t overflow in the html_escape length counter (len += 5/4/6/1 per char) or in malloc(len + 1) could undersize the buffer, but triggering it requires an input string approaching SIZE_MAX bytes (~2^64), which no statement in this code or realistic entry point can produce; no bound check exists, but the trigger is un-instantiable.

strcpy/strcat (CWE-676 pattern) are used in get_welcome_message, but the buffer total_length is computed exactly to the written byte count, verified by simulation for E=0 and general E; no overflow is reachable.

If a future maintainer changes one switch's entity constants without the other (e.g., count 5 but copy 6 bytes), an overflow would appear; the two switches must be kept in sync, but as written they match.

verdict.summary: nfs3svc_decode_writeargs never verifies that the parsed WRITE header fits inside the received head buffer. An NFSv3 client can send a call whose args area is shorter than the fixed header, so p advances past head->iov_len; then hdr > head->iov_len makes both `dlen = head->iov_len + page_len + tail->iov_len - hdr` and `rq_vec[0].iov_len = head->iov_len - hdr` wrap to huge unsigned values. The wrapped dlen defeats the `dlen < XDR_QUADLEN(len)*4` adequacy check (it must never be smaller, per the comment), the wrapped iov_len makes the vec-filling loop a no-op, and line 53 installs len (up to max_blocksize) as the length of a vector whose base p lies beyond the valid head data. The write path then reads up to max_blocksize bytes past the end of the head page and writes that out-of-bounds kernel memory into the attacker-chosen exported file, which the attacker reads back — a network-triggered kernel memory disclosure.

evidence.snippet:
hdr = (void*)p - head->iov_base;
	dlen = head->iov_len + rqstp->rq_arg.page_len + tail->iov_len - hdr;
evidence.reason: Nothing in the code checks hdr <= head->iov_len, even though the decode statements (lines 9-16) advance p up to ~88 bytes with no bounds test against head->iov_len. For an attacker-supplied call with a 12-byte args area, hdr = 24 > head->iov_len = 12, so `head->iov_len + page_len + tail->iov_len - hdr` wraps to 0xFFFFFFF4 and the guard `if (dlen < XDR_QUADLEN(len)*4)` at line 37 fails open, exactly violating the comment's invariant 'It must never be smaller.'

Same missing bound: with hdr = 24 and head->iov_len = 12, iov_len underflows to 0xFFFFFFF4, the while loop at line 47 is skipped (len <= max_blocksize is never > ~4G), and line 53 then sets rq_vec[0].iov_len = len (up to max_blocksize) with base p pointing past the end of the received data. The write path subsequently reads up to max_blocksize bytes starting at page+RPC-header+24, running off the end of the 4096-byte head page; the out-of-bounds kernel memory is written to the attacker-selected exported file and read back — instantiated OOB read/disclosure (CWE-125) caused by unsigned underflow (CWE-191).

assumptions: The sunrpc receive/dispatch path (svc_process, transport) is not shown; no quotable statement in the given code bounds rq_arg.head[0].iov_len from below per procedure, so a call whose args area is shorter than the ~24-88 byte WRITE header is treated as reachable — per guard anchoring, a 'framework guarantees enough head bytes' defense is an assumption, and this function is the intake point for the wire data.

svc_max_payload(rqstp) (line 5) is external; the clamp at lines 40-43 is assumed to keep the loop's index v within rq_vec[]/rq_pages[] capacity for the non-underflow paths. This does not affect the primary finding, whose trigger path skips the loop entirely.

The head buffer is assumed to be at least PAGE_SIZE so that the unbounded parse reads (lines 9, 12, 14-16) stay inside the page allocation; the primary defect does not depend on this (the OOB happens at the vec read, beyond the page).
limitations: XDR_QUADLEN(len)*4 wraps to 0 for len = 0xFFFFFFFD, independently defeating the dlen adequacy check (fail-open); after the clamp it yields a read of stale page memory rather than a cross-page OOB — secondary facet of the same missing validation, folded into the primary finding.
args->stable is not validated here; no memory-safety or authz consequence is instantiable within this code, so it is not a finding.
The unbounded parse reads beyond head->iov_len (lines 9-16) disclose stale bytes within the head page only; subsumed by the primary OOB-read finding.

verdict.summary: runDOMAttributeGetter is internal Blink glue with no memory-size/index arithmetic and no injection sinks. All observable value preconditions are guarded by quotable checks on every path (descriptor must be an object: '!descriptor->IsObject()'; getter must be a function: '!getter->IsFunction()'; both fail closed via RELEASE_NOTREACHED), and the function-call sink handles failure explicitly. The candidate defects (empty classObject from classObjectOfPrivateScript, an exception thrown by initializeHolderIfNeeded escaping the late-constructed v8::TryCatch at line 16, and attacker tampering with the private-script context) all have trigger preconditions that cannot be instantiated from the given code — they depend on helpers or isolation code not shown — and are recorded as limitations, not vulnerabilities.

assumptions: classObjectOfPrivateScript(scriptState, className), initializeHolderIfNeeded(...), rethrowExceptionInPrivateScript(...), v8String(...) and V8ScriptRunner::callInternalFunction(...) are not shown; their internal behavior (return values on failure, throwing operations, isolation of the private-script context from user JS) cannot be quoted and is treated as unknown, not as safe.
className and attributeName are treated as contract arguments (compile-time literals emitted by generated private-script bindings); in deployment no remote content flows into them.
The empty v8::Local return value at 'return v8::Local<v8::Value>();' is assumed to be handled by the generated caller, which is not shown.
limitations: Empty-handle deref: 'classObject->GetOwnPropertyDescriptor(...)' (line 6) executes without any check that classObject is non-empty; if classObjectOfPrivateScript could return an empty Local on failure, this would crash the renderer. The producing statement is in a helper not shown, so the trigger cannot be instantiated from this code.

TryCatch scope: 'v8::TryCatch block(isolate);' (line 16) is created AFTER 'initializeHolderIfNeeded(scriptState, classObject, holder);' (line 15). If line 15 could throw (e.g., under stack exhaustion), the exception escapes block's scope, line 18 invokes a function with a pending exception, and rethrowExceptionInPrivateScript at line 19 receives a TryCatch that caught nothing. The throwing statement inside the unshown helper could not be exhibited, so this is speculative. A minimal fix would move the TryCatch before line 15; no such check exists in this code.

Attacker tampering of the private-script context (replacing the getter reached via GetOwnPropertyDescriptor/Get(..., "get") to invoke an attacker-chosen function with holder as receiver) would be a type-confusion impact, but no path in this code lets user JS reach classObject; isolation is enforced in code not shown.

RELEASE_NOTREACHED() at lines 8 and 13 aborts the renderer if the descriptor or getter is genuinely missing; in a correctly built binary this indicates a Blink programming error, not attacker-reachable input, and is at worst a same-process crash.

verdict.summary: set_ssl_ciphers stores parsed algorithm IDs in a process-wide `static ALG_ID algIds[45]` and aliases that shared buffer into the caller's credential (`schannel_cred->palgSupportedAlgs = algIds`). Any subsequent invocation — from another thread concurrently or another connection sequentially — overwrites the array via `algIds[algCount++] = alg`, so a previously returned credential advertises a corrupted cipher list (including ciphers the first caller explicitly excluded). The corrupted credential is consumed by the TLS handshake, enabling weak-cipher negotiation with a hostile peer. The index bound `algCount < 45` is correctly enforced (no out-of-bounds write); the defect is the shared mutable state, which has no guard anywhere in the code.

evidence.snippet: static ALG_ID algIds[45]; /*There are 45 listed in the MS headers*/
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted state: the algorithm-ID buffer is `static`, i.e. shared process-global storage reused by every call to set_ssl_ciphers, so values parsed from one caller's `ciphers` string persist into and are overwritten by every other call.

Unguarded aliasing sink: the caller-owned credential is pointed at the shared static buffer with no copy, per-call allocation, or reuse protection anywhere in the function. Instantiated trigger: call 1 sets credA.cSupportedAlgs=5 with algIds[0..4]=A1..A5; a later call 2 executes `algIds[algCount++] = alg` writing algIds[0]=RC4, so credA (cSupportedAlgs still 5) advertises RC4 to the TLS peer — a weak-cipher downgrade across the network boundary; the same corruption occurs via interleaved writes from a concurrent thread (CWE-362).

assumptions: get_alg_id_by_name(startCur) is a helper not shown; its return value is assumed to be a valid ALG_ID for a recognized prefix, and its behavior cannot be quoted or relied on to reject any candidate.
schannel_cred is treated as a documented non-NULL contract argument; NULL-deref scenarios are contract questions, not attack data.
ALG_ID is assumed to be a 32-bit unsigned type per the Windows headers.
limitations: The loop bound `while(startCur && (0 != *startCur) && (algCount < 45))` correctly prevents out-of-bounds writes to algIds[45]: maximum write index is 44 (verified at the algCount=44/45 boundary), so the apparent 45-element overflow candidate is dismissed with the guard quoted.

Cipher-list entries beyond 45 are silently truncated (loop exits when algCount reaches 45 while the string continues); this is a configuration-surprise robustness issue with no boundary-crossing impact shown.
strtol returns long while algIds holds ALG_ID; values wider than 32 bits truncate, producing only a bogus-but-in-bounds algorithm constant passed to the OS credential API — no memory-safety effect.
A NULL-dereference of schannel_cred would require a caller violating the documented non-NULL contract, which is not instantiable from this code's own flow.

verdict.summary: The only attacker-influenced data reaching a sink is `len`, and its sole precondition enforceable inside this function — being a multiple of the block size — is guarded by `if (len % ctx->blocksize) { ... return -1; }` on every path to both nettle decrypt calls, before the use, with no wrap or unit confusion (all size_t, modulo only; len=0 is a harmless no-op, SIZE_MAX fails the modulo). All other candidates (NULL cipher, zero blocksize, encrypt-context fallback, out-buffer sizing) depend on caller contract violations or init-time state that no statement in this code produces.

assumptions: `ctx->blocksize` is set to a nonzero algorithm block size (>= 8) by the cipher init function (not shown); if it could be 0, line 6 would divide by zero, but no statement in this code produces that value.
`ctx->alg_decrypt` and at least one of `ctx->ctx_decrypt` / `ctx->ctx_encrypt` are non-NULL for any cipher object successfully created by init (not shown).
`in` and `out` buffers of at least `len` bytes are supplied by the caller per the documented public API contract; this function has no capacity parameter and cannot enforce it.
limitations: Missing NULL check on `cipher` before `cipher->opaque` (line 5): trigger requires a caller violating the documented non-NULL contract — contract issue, not attacker-data.
Potential division by zero at `len % ctx->blocksize` if blocksize were 0: requires init-produced state not shown; would crash the process at equal privilege — speculative robustness issue.

ECB/CBC paths fall back to `ctx->ctx_encrypt` when `ctx->ctx_decrypt` is NULL, which would apply the wrong key schedule for algorithms with distinct contexts; requires an init state this code cannot produce and yields wrong plaintext, not memory corruption or verification bypass.
No check that the `out` buffer is at least `len` bytes; this is the documented caller contract of this primitive API — the function has no allocation or capacity knowledge.

verdict.summary: get_welcome_message claims to escape the username for HTML output but the 'escape' is the identity assignment 'char* escaped_username = username;' — no HTML encoding, filtering, or transformation occurs. The raw attacker-controlled username is concatenated verbatim into the message (strcat(message, escaped_username)) which the documented contract states is rendered in an HTML page after login, enabling script/markup injection (XSS) into viewers' browsers. The buffer arithmetic itself is exact-fit and memory-safe; the sole defect is the absent output encoding.

evidence.snippet:
// Escape the username to prevent HTML injection
    char* escaped_username = username;
evidence.reason: The claimed HTML-escaping step is a no-op pointer assignment; escaped_username is byte-identical to the attacker-supplied username, so no guard exists between the tainted input and the HTML-bound output.

Sink: the unescaped attacker username (e.g. "<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>") is copied verbatim into the returned message that, per the function's documented contract, is rendered in an HTML page — instantiating HTML injection / XSS (CWE-79).

assumptions: The returned message is rendered in an HTML page, as stated in the function's documentation comment; the actual rendering site is not part of this translation unit.
The username can contain characters such as '<' and '>' in the deployment environment; this code performs no character validation that would preclude it.
limitations: size_t overflow in total_length (line 30) would require an input string near SIZE_MAX bytes; not instantiable here — the strcat sequence itself is exact-fit and memory-safe.
The printf calls use constant format strings, so no format-string vulnerability.
The commented-out free(escaped_username) calls are correctly inert: escaped_username aliases the caller's argv[1]; freeing it would itself be a double-free/invalid-free bug.

verdict.summary: The init function checks both allocation results (`if (!s->frame)` and `if (!s->vert_pred) return AVERROR(ENOMEM);`), so every hostile value of the attacker-influenced `avctx->width` that makes the size expression `s->avctx->width * sizeof(unsigned int)` unallocatable (negative, zero-ish via huge unsigned conversion, INT_MAX) routes to a checked ENOMEM return on the code's only path. A size wrap of the product to a small value is reachable only on 32-bit size_t targets with width in [2^30, 2^31), and the resulting out-of-bounds consumption would occur in decode code not present here, so that trigger is speculative and no primary vulnerability is instantiated in this code.

assumptions: `avctx` is non-NULL and `avctx->priv_data` is a valid, zero-allocated context per the FFmpeg codec framework contract; this code contains no such check (line 3 dereferences it directly).

`av_fast_malloc` either allocates at least min_size bytes or leaves `s->vert_pred` NULL on failure; this helper is not shown, but the line 11 NULL check makes the analysis independent of the exact failure semantics.
`avctx->width` is an int set from container metadata of an untrusted file before init; it is treated as attacker-data, and no statement in this code bounds it.
limitations: Speculative (CWE-190/CWE-131): `av_fast_malloc(&s->vert_pred, &s->vert_pred_size, s->avctx->width * sizeof(unsigned int));` (line 10) uses unvalidated attacker-influenced `width`; on a 32-bit size_t target, width in [2^30, 2^31) wraps the product to a small value and under-allocates `vert_pred` relative to `width` elements. Could not instantiate: the wrap requires a 32-bit build (on LP64 an int times 4 cannot wrap size_t, and all hostile widths hit the checked ENOMEM path), and the out-of-bounds read/write of `vert_pred` would occur in the decode loop, which is not part of the given code, so no consumption site could be quoted.

Speculative: `vert_pred` is sized exactly once at init from `avctx->width`; if the context width later changed to a larger value, a decode-time index into `vert_pred` would be out of bounds. Neither the width change nor any vert_pred indexing statement exists in the given code, so this precondition could not be instantiated.
Robustness only: on the line 12 ENOMEM path, `s->frame` is not freed by this function; at worst a transient allocation leak on an error return, with no cross-boundary security effect.

No range validation of `avctx->width` (e.g., width <= 0) exists anywhere in lines 1-14; inside this code the only consequences are a clean ENOMEM return or a benign padded allocation, so it is not a vulnerability here.

verdict.summary: display_dollar() uses its column parameter to index into the current line buffer without validating it against the line length: after only a negative clamp (col_arg < 0 ? 0 : col_arg), the value flows to (*mb_head_off)(p, p + col) with p = ml_get_curline(). mb_head_off dereferences its second argument and reads bytes at/after it, so any col greater than the length of the current line — reachable in Vim via 'virtualedit' cursor columns past end-of-line while editing an attacker-influenced buffer with a multi-byte encoding — causes a heap out-of-bounds read (crash under sanitizers; the resulting head offset also shifts the '$' display position, giving a small disclosure side channel on adjacent heap bytes). No statement in the function bounds col to STRLEN(p); the upstream fix is exactly the missing clamp.

evidence.reason: Root cause and sink: p + col indexes into the current line's text buffer, but col is never validated against the line's length; mb_head_off dereferences p + col (reading bytes at and after it). With col = 5 against a 2-byte line (reachable with a multi-byte 'encoding' and 'virtualedit' cursor columns past end-of-line while editing attacker-influenced buffer content), p + col points 3 bytes past the NUL terminator, producing a heap out-of-bounds read. No bound between col and STRLEN(p) exists on any path to this statement.

Origin of the tainted index: the only sanitization applied to the column parameter clamps negative values to 0, leaving any positive value up to INT_MAX unconstrained; this unbounded col reaches the p + col sink at line 18, and the missing upper-bound check against the current line length is the defective absence.

assumptions: colnr_T is a signed integer type (implied by the col_arg < 0 test on line 3); a negative wrap therefore cannot occur.
