mb_head_off (mbyte.c, not shown) dereferences its second argument and reads bytes at and following it (up to ~4 bytes for UTF-8) while locating the head byte, so passing a pointer past the end of the line buffer reads out of bounds.
ml_get_curline() (not shown) returns the current line's text, valid only for [p, p + STRLEN(p)] with the NUL at p + STRLEN(p).

Callers of display_dollar (Vim's insert-mode display code, not shown) pass a column derived from cursor/virtual position; under 'virtualedit' such columns legitimately exceed the physical line length, which is within this function's input domain — caller-side enforcement is not assumed.
limitations: No caller is shown, so the exact statement producing col > line length is outside this snippet; the finding rests on the parameter being attacker-data at this entry point and the total absence of an upper bound inside the function.
The out-of-bounds read distance is bounded (a few bytes for UTF-8) unless col is very large, in which case the wild read is more likely to crash the editor than disclose data.
curs_columns(FALSE) at line 20 receives the unbounded w_cursor.col = col; its internal handling cannot be audited from this snippet and is not counted as a finding.
The dismissed candidate 'w_cursor.col -= mb_head_off(...) can go negative' is impossible here because mb_head_off's return value is bounded by col (p - base = col).

verdict.summary: sanity_check_ckpt never validates raw_super->segment_count_main against total or total - fsmeta. main_segs is the sole upper bound for ckpt->cur_node_segno[i]/cur_data_segno[i] (lines 34/39), so a crafted f2fs image can declare segment_count_main near 2^32 on a tiny device and pass every check in this function with current-segment numbers far beyond the real segment count. Because this function is the mount-time validation intake for on-disk checkpoint metadata (attacker data crossing the user-to-kernel boundary), the missing consistency check allows out-of-bounds segment indexing in the kernel when the accepted checkpoint is used.

evidence.reason: The only bound applied to the attacker-controlled checkpoint segment numbers is main_segs, which itself is never validated against total or total - fsmeta. With segment_count_main = 0xFFFFF000 (line 30) on a device whose segment_count is 0x100, cur_node_segno[i] = 0x1000 passes this check and the function returns 0 at line 48, handing out-of-range segment numbers to the rest of f2fs for use as array indices (out-of-bounds kernel access). Trigger fully simulated in STEP 4.

Origin of the unvalidated value: segment_count_main is read directly from the attacker-supplied superblock image. No subsequent statement in this function compares main_segs with total (line 10) or with total - fsmeta (lines 11-18); the required guard is absent, so the bounds checks at lines 34-35 and 39-40 are vacuous for a crafted image.

assumptions: sbi->blocks_per_seg (line 31) is assumed to be validated by earlier superblock-parsing code (not shown in the given code); it cannot be quoted here, so it is not relied upon to dismiss anything.
raw_super and ckpt pointers are interface-contract arguments; non-NULL and initialized by earlier f2fs mount code (not shown).
F2FS_MIN_SEGMENTS is a compile-time constant (6); the FSM layout invariant total == fsmeta + main_segs is enforced nowhere in the given code.

The out-of-bounds use of the accepted segno values occurs in f2fs code outside this function; per the intake-point rule, this sanity-check function is the last validation layer for that on-disk data, so the missing check is assigned here.
limitations: The unsigned accumulation of fsmeta (lines 11-15) can wrap at 2^32-scale sums, letting absurd individual metadata counts pass the line 17 check; inside this function fsmeta only feeds comparisons, so this is recorded as part of the same missing-consistency class rather than a separate confirmed finding.
ovp_segments and reserved_segments (lines 20-21) are checked only for non-zero and are not bounded against total, but this function contains no sink consuming them.
Actual memory-corruption impact depends on downstream f2fs use of the accepted segment numbers, which is outside the given snippet; the confirmed defect is the absent validation at this intake point.

verdict.summary: This teardown routine consumes only internal decoder thread-management state (b_multithreaded_rd, allocated_decoding_thread_count, worker-thread arrays) and no attacker-data crosses its entry points, so no candidate trigger can be instantiated from the code as given. The loops that index h_event_start_decoding/h_decoding_thread by allocated_decoding_thread_count have no in-code size or NULL guard, but every harmful state (count exceeding initialized entries, NULL arrays with the flag set, concurrent double-free) must be produced by the setup routine or caller, none of which is in this code; re-entry is gated by 'pbi->b_multithreaded_rd = 0;' set before any free, so sequential double-free is impossible here.

assumptions: vpx_free is assumed to be a NULL-safe free wrapper (its implementation is not shown).

The invariant that, when b_multithreaded_rd == 1, h_decoding_thread and h_event_start_decoding are non-NULL and hold at least allocated_decoding_thread_count initialized entries is established by the thread-creation/setup routine (vp8_decoder_create_threads), which is not part of the given code and cannot be quoted or verified here.
pthread_join/sem_post/sem_destroy follow standard POSIX semantics; sem_post-then-join is assumed to let worker threads exit cleanly.
The caller invokes this function on a single thread per decoder context (decoder teardown is serialized by the API).
limitations: Out-of-bounds/invalid sem_post, pthread_join, and sem_destroy: if the setup routine sets allocated_decoding_thread_count before all sem_init/pthread_create calls succeed (a partial-failure path not shown), these loops would index uninitialized or out-of-extent array entries. The producing statements are not in this code, so the trigger is speculative here.

No NULL check on pbi, pbi->h_decoding_thread, or pbi->h_event_start_decoding before use (lines 12-13, 18); harm requires a setup failure leaving the flag set with NULL arrays — state not producible by statements in this code.
pbi->allocated_decoding_thread_count is not reset to 0 after teardown, leaving stale state; any exploitable interplay would occur in re-initialization code that is not shown.

Concurrent invocation could read b_multithreaded_rd before it is cleared and double-free the arrays; no lock exists, but no interleavable call sequence is exhibited within this code, so this is a caller-contract race, speculative here.
pbi itself is not NULL-checked; this is an interface-contract question (documented non-NULL context), not attack data.

verdict.summary: The only bounds check, `if (buf_offset + 32 >= sz)`, overflows its unsigned 64-bit arithmetic: for buf_offset values within 32 of 2^64 (e.g. 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFE6), the sum wraps to a small number and the check passes with as few as 7 bytes of buffer, after which `R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT (buffer, 6)` at line 11 reads one byte past the end of the heap buffer while parsing an attacker-supplied class file.

evidence.reason: This is the sole bounds check establishing the intended invariant that at least 33 bytes remain, but `buf_offset + 32` is ut64 arithmetic that wraps: with buf_offset = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFE6 the sum is 6, so 6 >= 7 is false and the check passes with sz = 7, leaving the downstream read at offset 6 unguarded.

Out-of-bounds read sink: with the wrapped guard bypassed (sz = 7, buf_offset = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFE6, offset = 6 after `offset += 6`), R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT(buffer, 6) reads buffer[6] and buffer[7], the latter one byte past the 7-byte heap buffer; the leaked byte becomes the annotation loop bound, letting adjacent heap memory influence control flow.

assumptions: len(buffer) == sz is the code's own internal model, inferred from line 18 passing `sz - offset` as the remaining size of the slice `buffer + offset`; no explicit statement states it.

r_bin_java_default_attr_new (line 7, not shown) is assumed to parse the 6-byte attribute header from the in-bounds prefix of a 7-byte buffer and return a non-NULL attr without an independent size rejection; no such rejection can be quoted from the shown code.

buf_offset is treated as attacker-derived (an offset computed from walking the attacker's class file); whether the caller's offset arithmetic (not shown) can actually produce a wrap-region value near 2^64 cannot be verified from this code, and no quotable bound on it exists here.
limitations: Union-member inconsistency: num_annotations is written via `attr->info.annotation_array.num_annotations` (line 11) but the loop bound is read from `attr->info.rtv_annotations_attr.num_annotations` (line 14) in an rti function; if the two members have differing layouts and the attr is not zero-initialized this would be an uninitialized loop bound (CWE-457), but the struct definitions are not shown so the trigger could not be instantiated — speculative.

`offset += annotation->size;` (line 20) trusts a callee-produced size; an overshoot is caught by the line 15 re-check and a wrap keeps subsequent slices in-bounds, so no out-of-bounds access within this function could be instantiated without assuming annotation_new internals (not shown).
NULL annotations are appended to the list (line 22) and `attr->size = offset` (line 24) may exceed sz after an oversize final annotation; both only matter in consumers not shown.

A failing r_bin_java_annotation_new leaves offset unadvanced but the loop is bounded by num_annotations (ut16 read), so at most 65535 stalled iterations — bounded, not attacker-scalable amplification.

verdict.summary: unix_getpw dereferences encrypted_pass at 'if (encrypted_pass[0] == 0)' without any NULL check on the paths where it was assigned from 'encrypted_pass = pwd->pw_passwd;' (no HAVE_GETSPNAM build) or 'encrypted_pass = spwd->sp_pwdp;' (shadow build: the only NULL test, 'if ((encrypted_pass == NULL) || ...)', runs before the reassignment and does not re-validate sp_pwdp). A network peer sending an Access-Request whose User-Name resolves to a passwd/shadow entry with a NULL password pointer crashes the privileged, shared radiusd process (denial of service of the authentication service).

evidence.reason: Sink: unconditional array dereference of encrypted_pass. No NULL check exists on any path from the assignments at lines 45/62 to this statement (the only NULL test, at line 58, precedes the line-62 reassignment and is compiled out without HAVE_GETSPNAM). Trigger: attacker-supplied User-Name resolves to a lookup entry whose password field is a NULL pointer, producing a NULL dereference (CWE-476) and crash of the network-facing radiusd daemon.

Origin: the only NULL guard on encrypted_pass checks the value BEFORE the shadow lookup and only routes to getspnam; the reassignment 'encrypted_pass = spwd->sp_pwdp;' is not NULL-checked (only the struct pointer spwd is), so a NULL field pointer flows unvalidated to the dereference at line 136.

assumptions: Compile-time configuration assumed to be the mainstream shadow build (HAVE_GETSPNAM and HAVE_GETUSERSHELL defined, OSFC2 undefined); no #define values are given in the code.
request->username->vp_strvalue is the User-Name from a network RADIUS Access-Request and is attacker-controlled content; request and vp_list pointers are otherwise interface-contract inputs.

getpwnam/getspnam are trusted libc lookups keyed by attacker data; the possibility that their password-field pointers (pw_passwd, sp_pwdp) are NULL is treated as a real return state because the code's own comment (lines 52-56) explicitly anticipates 'NULL password fields'.
limitations: On glibc's local-files NSS backend an empty password field is typically parsed as an empty string rather than NULL, in which case line 136 returns NOOP instead of crashing; the NULL-field trigger depends on the NSS/passwd source (e.g., NIS-style entries), so exploitability is host-configuration dependent even though the missing NULL check is definitively absent from the code.

OSFC2-only: line 37 'if (pr_pw->uflg.fg_lock!=1)' appears to test the field-validity flag rather than the lock value fd_lock, suggesting locked accounts (fg_lock==1, fd_lock set) are not rejected — a potential lock bypass (CWE-863). Not counted as primary: the OSFC2 build and the exact platform semantics of fg_lock cannot be instantiated from the given code.
strcmp against pwd->pw_shell (lines 74/87) could crash if pw_shell is NULL; same libc-dependent conditionality, no in-code instantiation.

Shadow expiry/account-expiry checks (lines 105-117) are skipped when spwd is NULL because the passwd file held a >=10-character hash; this is a configuration-dependent logic weakness acknowledged by the code's own comment and has no trigger instantiable from the given code.

verdict.summary: jpc_pi_nextrpcl computes pi->prcno = prcvind * numhprcs + prchind from attacker-controlled codestream geometry (image/tile coordinates, sampling factors, precinct exponents) and uses it to index the heap array pi->pirlvl->prclyrnos without any runtime bounds check; the only 'guard' is assert(pi->prcno < pi->pirlvl->numprcs), which is compiled out in release builds, does not reject negative indices, and aborts rather than validates. A crafted JPEG2000 file yields prcno >= numprcs (or negative), causing an out-of-bounds read at *prclyrno and an out-of-bounds heap write via ++(*prclyrno) — memory corruption in the process decoding untrusted data.

evidence.reason: Sink: pi->prcno, derived from attacker-controlled coordinates and precinct-grid values, indexes prclyrnos (allocated with numprcs entries). With prcno >= numprcs (e.g., x iterated past the precinct grid: prchind = numhprcs), line 87 reads one-past-end and line 89 increments out of bounds — heap OOB read and write.

Origin of the tainted index: prcvind/prchind are computed (lines 75-80) from pi->x/pi->y, hsamp/vsamp, r, and precinct exponents, all from the codestream; nothing in this function bounds the product/sum against pi->pirlvl->numprcs, and it can also wrap negative via int truncation of unsigned arithmetic.

The only check relating prcno to numprcs is this assert — compiled out under the standard NDEBUG release configuration, not a rejection path, and it omits the prcno < 0 case; the minimal fix (if (pi->prcno < 0 || pi->prcno >= pi->pirlvl->numprcs) continue;) appears nowhere in the code.

assumptions: assert() is removed in NDEBUG release builds; even when active it aborts rather than validates, and does not check prcno >= 0.

The size of pi->pirlvl->prclyrnos and the computation of numhprcs/numprcs occur in code not shown; no statement in this function establishes any relation between pi->prcno and numprcs other than the assert, so their consistency cannot be relied on per guard anchoring.
JPC_CEILDIV/JPC_FLOORDIVPOW2 are the usual unsigned ceil-division / floor-power-of-2 macros; JAS_UINTFAST32_NUMBITS is the width of uint_fast32_t.
limitations: Speculative: division by zero at 'pi->ystep - (pi->y % pi->ystep)' / 'pi->xstep - (pi->x % pi->xstep)' (lines 49-52) if xstep/ystep truncate to 0 — the shift guard at lines 30-33 permits prcwidthexpn + numrlvls up to JAS_UINTFAST32_NUMBITS - 2 (up to 61 on LP64), so 1 << shift assigned to the int locals xstep/ystep can truncate to 0, and hsamp == 0 also yields xstep 0; reachability depends on decoder-side caps not shown and on the platform width of uint_fast32_t, so this candidate was not counted as primary.
The OOB access is a confirmed primary only via C1; candidates requiring a specific 32-bit target or a race window were not instantiated.

verdict.summary: mov_read_stsz indexes c->fc->streams[c->fc->nb_streams-1] with no check that nb_streams >= 1. An attacker-supplied MOV/MP4 file that places an stsz atom before any stream-creating atom invokes this handler with nb_streams == 0, producing a streams[-1] out-of-bounds pointer read whose result is dereferenced (st->priv_data) and written through (sc->sample_size, sc->sample_count, sc->sample_sizes[i]) — memory corruption/crash in the process decoding untrusted content. Additionally, the allocation and parse loop are sized solely by the attacker-controlled 'entries' field with no check against atom.size or remaining bytes: a 16-byte stsz atom with entries = 536870910 (passing the overflow guard at lines 11-12) forces a ~4.3 GiB allocation and 5.4x10^8 loop iterations, an attacker-scalable amplification (CWE-400).

evidence.reason: Root cause: the very first statement indexes streams[nb_streams-1] with no guard that nb_streams >= 1 (no such check exists anywhere in the function, and no statement here creates a stream). Trigger: attacker file whose first atom is stsz, so the handler runs with c->fc->nb_streams == 0; index = 0-1 = -1 gives an out-of-bounds read of streams[-1]; the resulting wild pointer is dereferenced at st->priv_data and then written through at sc->sample_size = get_be32(pb) (line 9) and sc->sample_count = entries (line 13) — OOB read (CWE-125) with memory-corruption/wild-write potential in the process consuming untrusted content.

Root cause: both the allocation size and the loop bound are derived solely from the attacker-controlled 32-bit 'entries' field (line 10) with no comparison against atom.size or bytes remaining in pb; the only guard (lines 11-12) bounds integer overflow, not consumption. Trigger: a 16-byte stsz atom with sample_size = 0 and entries = 536870910 passes the guard, forces av_malloc of ~4.3 GiB retained for the stream's lifetime and 536,870,910 loop iterations of get_be32 — small input producing attacker-scalable work and retention (CWE-400).

assumptions: The stsz handler is reachable via the demuxer's atom dispatch on an stsz fourcc at the position the attacker's file places it; the dispatch table and mov_read_default are not shown, so reachability with nb_streams == 0 (stsz before any trak/stsd) is inferred from the attacker controlling atom ordering, not quoted from shown code.

get_be32/get_byte behavior at end-of-stream (old FFmpeg ByteIOContext returns 0 past EOF) is not shown; the CWE-400 finding rests on the committed allocation size and loop count, not on read behavior past EOF.
sizeof(long) assumed 4 or 8; the overflow guard at lines 11-12 is correct under both widths, so the platform width only scales the CWE-400 allocation between ~4 GiB and ~4 GiB.
sc->sample_sizes is assumed freed by the demuxer teardown elsewhere (not shown).
limitations: Integer overflow in entries * sizeof(long) is genuinely guarded by 'if(entries >= UINT_MAX / sizeof(long)) return -1;' (lines 11-12); edge-tested at entries == UINT_MAX/sizeof(long) exactly and one below: no wrap occurs on 32- or 64-bit targets.
Allocation failure is checked: 'if (!sc->sample_sizes) return -1;' — no unchecked-malloc dereference.
The loop writes sc->sample_sizes[i] for i < entries into a buffer of exactly entries elements, so no heap overflow exists in the fill loop.

If the host application only ever invokes this handler after a stream is guaranteed to exist (a constraint no shown statement enforces), candidate 1 would reduce to a contract question; per guard-anchoring that enforcement cannot be quoted here, so the candidate stands.

verdict.summary: The attacker-controlled numSpecs value is fully guarded against integer overflow before its product with sizeof(spec) is used as the request-length check: 'if (stuff->numSpecs > UINT32_MAX / sizeof(ctx.specs[0])) return BadLength;' bounds the product below 2^32 on every path, and REQUEST_FIXED_SIZE then requires the received request length to match exactly before the spec buffer is used. Remaining concerns (32-bit wrap inside the not-shown REQUEST_FIXED_SIZE macro arithmetic, ctx initialization on a truncated snippet line, bytes_to_int32 truncation of callee-computed resultBytes, and a possible leak on the BadAlloc path) all depend on code outside the given snippet and could not be instantiated as triggers in this code.

assumptions: REQUEST_FIXED_SIZE and REQUEST_AT_LEAST_SIZE are the standard X-Server request-length macros; their bodies are not part of the given code, so their exact comparison width and arithmetic are assumed, not verified here.

The line initializing ctx (a ConstructResourceBytesCtx_init-style call taking stuff->client, the spec count, and (void*)((char*)stuff + sz_xXResQueryResourceBytesReq), with 'return BadAlloc' on failure) is truncated out of the given snippet; the visible dangling fragment '... sz_xXResQueryResourceBytesReq))) { return BadAlloc; }' implies a checked init exists. As literally printed the snippet does not compile.
ConstructResourceBytes, DestroyConstructResourceBytesCtx, SwapXResQueryResourceBytes, and WriteFragmentsToClient are treated as correctly implemented per their contracts; their bodies are not shown.
The X-Server dispatcher bounds the actual request buffer to the length field before this handler runs.
limitations: A 32-bit-size_t build could wrap 'sizeof(req) + numSpecs*sizeof(spec)' (numSpecs at the guard's exact limit 0x1FFFFFFF gives 12 + 0xFFFFFFF8 = 0x100000004) inside the REQUEST_FIXED_SIZE macro, which is not part of the given code; the resulting out-of-bounds spec walk would occur in the unshown ctx-init/callee. Speculative: trigger precondition (32-bit target + macro-internal wrap) cannot be instantiated from the given statements.

ctx.resultBytes >= 4 GiB would truncate via bytes_to_int32 into the 32-bit reply length field, but resultBytes is computed by the unshown ConstructResourceBytes over server-managed resource sizes; not instantiated here.
The 'return BadAlloc' path skips DestroyConstructResourceBytesCtx, which may leak whatever the (unshown) init allocated; not provable from the given code.

The truncated init line makes literal compilation impossible; if the init call were genuinely absent, ctx would be used uninitialized (CWE-457-style disclosure), but the fragment shows a checked init exists in the original source.

verdict.summary: pcmk_process_exit is an internal, static child-exit handler in the pacemaker daemon. All values it consumes (the child-table entry, its name/flags, local_nodeid, shutdown_trigger, and the PCMK_fail_fast environment variable set at daemon launch) originate inside the operator-controlled daemon, not across a trust boundary. All logging calls use constant format strings with %s-bound trusted arguments; the only NULL-sensitive call (mainloop_set_trigger) is guarded by 'if (shutdown_trigger)'. The only arithmetic (respawn_count += 1) cannot reach its type boundary within any instantiable trigger, since each increment requires a real child process death and respawn is disabled after MAX_RESPAWN. No attacker-data path reaches a memory, format, command, or authorization sink.

assumptions: child points to a valid, statically allocated entry of the daemon's own process table; the caller is the same file's child-exit dispatch (contract argument, static function).
child->name is a string constant from the daemon's built-in child table; no external data populates it in this code.
PCMK_fail_fast is set in the daemon's launch environment by the operator; this code contains no path by which a network peer or tenant sets it.
The declared widths of respawn_count and MAX_RESPAWN are not shown; the overflow analysis assumes at least a 32-bit signed integer, which only makes the candidate harder to trigger.
limitations: child->respawn_count += 1 has no saturation check; a theoretical signed-overflow (UB) would require on the order of 2^31 actual child-process exits after respawn is already disabled at MAX_RESPAWN — not instantiable by any input to this code; robustness note only.
child is dereferenced without a NULL check; trigger would require the internal static caller to violate its contract; not attacker-reachable.

If PCMK_fail_fast were attacker-controllable in some deployment (e.g., a privileged daemon launched from an attacker-writable service definition), the pcmk_panic reboot path would be attacker-influenced; that control lies outside this code's input surface.

verdict.summary: pcmk_process_exit is a process-supervision routine whose inputs (internal pcmk_child_t state, module globals, and the operator-set PCMK_fail_fast environment variable) do not cross a trust boundary within this code. All logging call sites use constant literal format strings with correctly paired %s arguments, the repeated-timer registration is guarded by 'if (!global_keep_tracking)', and no memory, allocation, index, copy, injection, or crypto sink is reached by any value lacking an enforceable precondition. The only behavioral nuance is an off-by-one in the respawn cap ('>' vs '>=') whose worst consequence is one additional supervised respawn attempt of a local daemon child, confined to the equal-privilege supervisor process.

assumptions: The declared type/width of child->respawn_count is not visible in this excerpt; overflow analysis is therefore recorded as an assumption rather than a fact. Even on wrap, the value reaches only a comparison and a boolean write, not a memory/index/size sink.

pcmk_panic, start_child, update_node_processes, get_process_list, pcmk_child_active, and check_active_before_startup_processes are external helpers whose internals are not shown; their arguments here are internal daemon state, and none is invoked with a boundary-crossing value.
limitations: Off-by-one: 'if (child->respawn_count > MAX_RESPAWN)' uses '>' instead of '>=', so respawn is disabled only at MAX_RESPAWN+1, permitting exactly one extra supervised respawn attempt. Consequence is bounded (the next death sets respawn = FALSE) and confined to the node's own privileged supervisor; classified as robustness, not security impact.
child->respawn_count += 1 could in principle wrap if the counter type is narrow, but the type is not declared here and no code shown can produce the wrap value; speculative.

crm_warn passes child->endpoint to %s; if endpoint were NULL, output would be platform-dependent ('(null)' on glibc). endpoint is daemon-internal state, not attacker data, so this is a robustness note only.

The PCMK_fail_fast environment variable triggers a system reboot on child death; this is operator configuration of the daemon's own environment, not attacker-controlled input across a service boundary.

verdict.summary: mov_read_stsz reads the attacker-controlled 32-bit field 'entries' directly from the media file (line 10) and uses it without any bound or sign check to size a heap allocation, entries * sizeof(long) (line 17). On builds where the size_t product wraps (entries >= 2^30 with 32-bit size_t), av_malloc returns a tiny buffer while the loop at lines 20-21 writes 'entries' longs into it, a remotely triggerable heap buffer overflow with attacker file content. Even where the product does not wrap, the unbounded 'entries' (up to 2^31-1) drives an attacker-scaled multi-GB allocation and ~2^31-iteration loop from a 4-byte input, with no validation against the atom's remaining size.

evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: 'entries' is a signed int populated with an arbitrary 32-bit value from the attacker-controlled media file; no sign, range, or atom-size validation is applied to it anywhere in the function.

Defective allocation sizing: entries * sizeof(long) wraps (integer overflow, CWE-190) for entries >= 2^30 when computed in a 32-bit size_t, yielding a grossly undersized heap buffer (e.g., entries = 0x40000001 allocates 4 bytes); the only guard, 'if (!sc->sample_sizes)' at line 18, checks the result, not the size arithmetic, and the 'if(sc->sample_size)' branch at line 15 tests a different variable.

Out-of-bounds heap write sink (CWE-787): the loop bound is the unvalidated attacker value 'entries', and each iteration writes one long at sc->sample_sizes[i]; with the wrapped allocation from line 17 the first write at i=1 (byte offset 4 of a 4-byte block) is already out of bounds, and ~10^9 further attacker-file-derived words are written past the buffer.

assumptions: av_malloc's parameter width and its behavior on size 0 are not shown in the given code; historically ffmpeg's av_malloc took an 'unsigned int' size, which would also truncate entries * sizeof(long) on 64-bit builds, but this analysis relies only on the 32-bit size_t wrap, which occurs in the given expression itself.

The atom dispatch table that invokes mov_read_stsz, the behavior of get_be32 at end-of-file, and the allocation of st->priv_data during stream creation are outside the given code; nothing about them is used to dismiss a candidate.
limitations: On LP64 builds the product entries * sizeof(long) (max ~16 GB) does not wrap in 64-bit size_t; the observable defect there is attacker-scalable resource consumption (CWE-400): a 4-byte 'entries' field drives up to a 16 GB allocation attempt and up to 2^31 loop iterations with no check that entries fits the atom's remaining size — a remotely triggerable memory-exhaustion/CPU DoS, not memory corruption.

Speculative, not counted: 'c->fc->streams[c->fc->nb_streams-1]' at line 3 indexes with -1 if nb_streams == 0 (OOB read / wild pointer deref). The precondition nb_streams==0 requires the atom dispatcher (not shown) to route a stsz atom before any trak atom; no statement in this code produces that state, so the trigger could not be fully instantiated here.
Speculative/contract: st->priv_data being NULL depends on stream-creation code outside this function; not attacker data within this code's own flow.
Negative 'entries' values convert to SIZE_MAX-scale sizes that fail allocation (line 18 returns -1) and skip the loop, so they do not trigger the overflow.

verdict.summary: rv10_decode_packet() passes unvalidated end coordinates to ff_er_add_slice(): after the decode loop the macroblock position can wrap to (mb_x=0, mb_y=mb_height) (one-past the frame in both dimensions), so line 100 calls ff_er_add_slice with endx = s->mb_x-1 = -1 and endy = s->mb_y = mb_height. The pre-loop bounds check (lines 15-19) does not run after the loop and no guard exists between the wrap (lines 91-93) and the call, yielding an attacker-driven out-of-bounds write in the per-macroblock error-status table while decoding an untrusted RV10/RV20 stream.

evidence.snippet: ff_er_add_slice(s, start_mb_x, s->resync_mb_y, s->mb_x-1, s->mb_y, AC_END|DC_END|MV_END);
evidence.reason: Unguarded sink: the end coordinates s->mb_x-1 and s->mb_y are passed to ff_er_add_slice without any post-loop bounds check, although s->mb_x can be 0 (making endx = -1) and s->mb_y can equal s->mb_height (one past the last macroblock row). The attacker controls mb_count and the macroblock payload via the packet bits, so a full-frame slice (mb_count == mb_width*mb_height starting at (0,0)) or mb_count == 0 with mb_x == 0 drives out-of-frame coordinates into the slice/error-status writer, causing an out-of-bounds write (root cause: missing validation of macroblock index/coordinate, CWE-787/CWE-129).

Origin of the tainted coordinates: on the final loop iteration (permitted because the check 'if (mb_count > left)' allows mb_count == left == mb_width*mb_height) this wrap sets s->mb_x = 0 and s->mb_y = mb_height exactly when the loop exits, producing the out-of-frame values (-1, mb_height) consumed at line 100.

assumptions: s->mb_width and s->mb_height are assumed positive and consistent with the allocated picture/error_status_table dimensions (enforced in ff_MPV_common_init, not shown); the trigger simulation works for any valid positive dimensions.

ff_er_add_slice(), ff_h263_decode_mb(), init_get_bits() and the picture-header decoders are not shown; per guard-anchoring discipline, no internal validation they may perform was used to dismiss the candidate at the line-100 call site.
SLICE_OK/SLICE_END/SLICE_ERROR semantics and the availability of clean-decoding macroblock payloads (needed for the full-frame trigger) are taken as the standard h263 decode contract.
limitations: Speculative: 'init_get_bits(&s->gb, buf, buf_size*8)' (line 6) has no guard on buf_size, and buf_size*8 overflows int for buf_size >= 2^28 (256MB). No statement in this code bounds buf_size and the demuxer/init_get_bits path is not shown, so the trigger precondition (a >=256MB packet reaching the decoder) could not be instantiated from this code alone.

Speculative: a negative s->mb_x/s->mb_y coming out of rv10/rv20_decode_picture_header would bypass the '>= ' checks at lines 15-19 (they do not reject negatives); no statement in this code produces a negative value, so it remains a contract question about the not-shown header parsers.
Candidate 2 and 3 above did not drive the verdict; only the line-100 ff_er_add_slice candidate was confirmed as primary.

verdict.summary: create_dump_dir_from_problem_data is an intake point for untrusted problem_data. For items with CD_FLAG_BIN, the attacker-controlled value->content is used directly as the source path of copy_file (line 92) with no validation anywhere in the loop (only the destination name is checked at line 82), so an unprivileged party can have the process (a privileged/shared abrt daemon in this code's deployment) read and copy an arbitrary attacker-named file into a dump dir made world-readable via S_IROTH — a disclosure crossing the trust boundary. Additionally, the uid validation at line 28 checks only the upper bound (INT_MAX < val) and then casts long→uid_t at line 34, so negative attacker-supplied uid strings wrap to huge unsigned uids (and '-1' aliases the 'unspecified' sentinel), letting the attacker set an out-of-range uid on the created dump directory.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled value->content (a CD_FLAG_BIN problem-data item iterated from the untrusted problem_data table) is used directly as the source path of copy_file with no validation; the only check in the loop, 'if (!str_is_correct_filename(name))' at line 82, validates the destination name only. The process reads the attacker-chosen file and writes a copy with the world-readable bit S_IROTH into the dump dir; trigger instantiated with item {name="coredump", flags=CD_FLAG_BIN, content="/etc/shadow"} reaching line 92 with no guard on any path.

Taint origin: name, value->flags and value->content are drawn from the problem_data hash table passed as the public function's first parameter, which carries external content across the trust boundary; these values reach the copy_file sink at line 92 unvalidated.

The uid validation enforces only an upper bound ('INT_MAX < val'); there is no lower-bound check, and the immediately following cast 'uid = (uid_t)val' converts a signed long to unsigned uid_t. Trigger: attacker-supplied FILENAME_UID="-2" passes the guard (errno==0, *endptr=='\0', INT_MAX < -2 is false) and becomes uid 4294967294, which is then passed as the ownership uid to try_dd_create at lines 50/54/63/70 — an attacker-chosen out-of-range uid governing dump-dir ownership and downstream access control.

assumptions: Helper implementations are not shown: copy_file is assumed to copy the file at its first (source path) argument; try_dd_create/dd_create are assumed to create the dump dir recording/chowning the passed uid; str_is_correct_filename is assumed to reject path separators and control characters in names; concat_path_file, dd_save_text, dd_create_basic_files, dd_rename semantics assumed per their names. None of these may validate attacker data on this code's behalf.

Security impact of the copy_file finding assumes this library function is invoked in a privileged or shared context (e.g., the abrt daemon creating user problem dirs under /var/run/abrt, as the code's own fallback at line 54 and its abrt-specific comments indicate), so that reading an attacker-chosen path discloses data the attacker cannot otherwise read; if invoked only by same-privilege callers on their own data, the copy alone would be harmless, though the uid finding remains an ownership/authorization defect.
NEW_PD_SUFFIX is assumed to be a non-empty constant string, making the suffix strip at line 112 in-bounds by construction.
uid_t is assumed to be a 32-bit unsigned type and long to be at least 32 bits, per POSIX/Linux.
limitations: Speculative: base_dir_name == NULL is explicitly supported (line 49 'if (base_dir_name)') but is later passed unconditionally to concat_path_file at line 113; if that helper does not tolerate NULL this is a NULL-deref crash (DoS of the daemon) or a bogus rename target. The helper's NULL handling is not shown, so the trigger could not be instantiated from the given code.
Speculative: TOCTOU/symlink behavior inside copy_file and try_dd_create depends on helper internals not shown.
Not security-relevant: 'new_path' (line 113) is never freed (memory leak); the '%li' format paired with (unsigned long) at line 96 is a cosmetic format mismatch.

The guard's acceptance of uid values 0..INT_MAX is arguably by-design trust in the caller; the confirmed defect is specifically the missing lower bound combined with the signed-to-unsigned cast, not the general trust of the UID field.

verdict.summary: The code writes the congratulation message with snprintf(buffer, buffer_size, ...), where buffer_size is the fixed 30-byte buffer size supplied at line 28, so the copy is intrinsically bounded and NUL-terminated even for arbitrarily long usernames. The format string is a constant literal, and argv[1] is only consumed as a %s argument. The unused userName_size parameter is dead code with no security consequence. No memory-safety, injection, or trust-boundary defect exists in this code.

assumptions: Standard C library snprintf semantics are assumed: it writes at most buffer_size bytes including the terminator and always NUL-terminates within that bound, even on truncation. This is the documented behavior of the function used at line 15.
buffer_size arrives as sizeof(buffer) = 30 (positive, small int) per lines 27-28; a negative or oversized size argument cannot be produced by any path in this code.
limitations: userName_size (line 12) is never read; the function ignores it. This is a dead-parameter code-quality issue, not a security defect, since snprintf enforces the bound regardless.
Long usernames cause the message to be truncated at 29 characters; this is snprintf's intended bounded behavior and has only cosmetic effect.

Even a hypothetical crash here would be confined to the equal-privilege CLI process of the user supplying argv[1], which per the attacker/impact model would be a robustness bug rather than a vulnerability; in fact no crash occurs because snprintf bounds all writes.

verdict.summary: write_refcount_block_entries validates only the lower bound of first_index (`first_index < 0`) but performs no upper-bound check of first_index or last_index against the refcount_block_cache allocation, and computes `size = (last_index - first_index) << REFCOUNT_SHIFT` from the unchecked `last_index + REFCOUNTS_PER_SECTOR` (signed overflow). Image-metadata-derived indices can therefore drive bdrv_pwrite to read past the end of s->refcount_block_cache and persist host heap bytes into the image file (out-of-bounds read with disclosure potential), or produce a wrap-induced oversized size.

evidence.reason: Root cause: no upper-bound validation of first_index/last_index against the refcount_block_cache allocation and no overflow check on `last_index + REFCOUNTS_PER_SECTOR`; the only guard is `if (first_index < 0) return 0;` (lines 10-11). With an image-derived first_index at/above the cache entry count, or last_index = INT_MAX making the addition wrap, `bdrv_pwrite` reads out of bounds from `s->refcount_block_cache[first_index]` for `size` bytes and writes them into the qcow2 image, disclosing host memory to the image provider.

evidence.snippet:
static int write_refcount_block_entries(BlockDriverState *bs,
    int64_t refcount_block_offset, int first_index, int last_index)
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values: first_index, last_index and refcount_block_offset are derived from qcow2 image metadata/cluster indexes (attacker-supplied image content) and enter this function unvalidated with respect to the cache allocation size.

assumptions: REFCOUNTS_PER_SECTOR is a power of two so the masking at lines 13-15 is an alignment round; REFCOUNT_SHIFT scales entries to bytes.
s->refcount_block_cache is a fixed-size buffer (allocated elsewhere in this translation unit's driver) whose entry count is not re-derived here; no bound against it exists in this code.

first_index/last_index originate from callers computing refcount entry indexes for clusters described by the (attacker-controlled) qcow2 image being written; the function is the last validation point for these values.
limitations: refcount_block_offset is not range-checked, allowing writes at attacker-chosen offsets within the image file; since the attacker already controls that file's content, this is image self-corruption rather than a cross-boundary write, and is not counted as primary.
Cache-write bypass when cache_refcount_updates is set (line 7) merely defers updates, no security effect.
Exact reachability of specific index values depends on the (not shown) callers in the qcow2 driver; the defect analyzed is the absence of any bounds/overflow guard in this function itself.

verdict.summary: No security vulnerability with an instantiable trigger exists in the given code. The dominant sink is fdata[fx] indexed by values returned solely by rpmfiNext, whose bound (0 <= fx < fc) is not checked in this listing but is the documented contract of the not-shown helper; no statement in this code can produce an out-of-range index, and every other candidate (failedFile NULL write, xcalloc sizing with attacker fc, filesystem TOCTOU, package-path writes) requires either a caller/callee contract violation, an unquotable external enforcement, or an attacker-writable filesystem location this code's own statements (0700 directories, suffixed temp names) do not create.

assumptions: rpmfiNext(fi) is assumed to return only valid file indices (0 <= fx < rpmfilesFC) or negative error codes; this bound is enforced inside the helper (not shown), not in the given code. It is therefore not quotable and is not used to dismiss any proven defect, but it is also the sole producer of fx, so no in-code trigger exists for an fdata[fx] out-of-bounds access.
rpmfilesFC(files) is assumed to return a non-negative file count validated during header parsing (helper not shown); a negative or overflowing fc cannot be produced by any statement in this listing.

xcalloc/rasprintf/xstrdup are assumed to be rpm's checked allocators (abort on failure, non-NULL for zero-size), and fdOp/Fclose/rpmfiFree are assumed NULL-tolerant; these live outside the given code.

Speculative: TOCTOU between fsmStat/fsmVerify and fsmSetmeta/fsmCommit exists by design, but package-created directories are created 0700 (mode |= 00700) and new files carry a transaction-specific suffix until an atomic rename, so an attacker able to interleave must already control a writable directory this code never creates.

Robustness only: *failedFile is overwritten on later failures without freeing the prior value (bounded memory leak per transaction), and firstlinkfile FD closure on error paths cannot be verified from the shown code.

Process-termination scenarios driven solely by operator-supplied allocation failure or a malformed package already accepted for install (equal-privilege/administrative trust decision) are robustness issues, not boundary-crossing vulnerabilities.

verdict.summary: This JNI function is a thin forwarder: it passes env, a caller-supplied constant-pool object handle, and a caller-supplied jint cpIndex straight to getFieldAt() with a fixed resolve flag. The function body performs no memory access, arithmetic, indexing, or other sink on the data-carrying parameters; any bounds validation or dereference of cpIndex/constantPoolOop occurs inside getFieldAt, whose body is not part of the given code. No defect can be instantiated within this snippet.

assumptions: Bounds checking of cpIndex (a 32-bit signed index) and type/NULL validation of constantPoolOop is assumed to occur inside getFieldAt(), which is not included in the given code; per guard anchoring, no such check can be quoted from the given code.

The practical callers of Java_sun_reflect_ConstantPool_getFieldAtIfLoaded0 are JDK-internal reflection components (sun.reflect.ConstantPool is not a public API), so cpIndex values typically originate from class-file parsing of loaded classes rather than arbitrary untrusted input; this was not used to dismiss any in-code sink, as none exists.
limitations: Candidate: unchecked cpIndex could cause an out-of-bounds read of the constant pool inside getFieldAt (potential CWE-125). This is speculative for the given snippet because the indexing sink does not exist in this code; the only statement is 'return getFieldAt(env, constantPoolOop, cpIndex, J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_NO_CLASS_LOAD);'. If getFieldAt's body lacks a bounds check on cpIndex, the vulnerability belongs to that body, not this function.
Candidate: constantPoolOop NULL or wrong-type handle — interface-contract question for the callee; no use site in this code.
No arithmetic, copy, allocation, format, command, path, or crypto sinks exist in the snippet, so no further candidates could be generated.

verdict.summary: virgl_cmd_get_capset fills gc from the guest-supplied control command (line 7), then sizes the response buffer solely from virgl_renderer_get_cap_set's id-only query result (max_size, line 14) while passing the never-validated, guest-controlled gc.capset_version to virgl_renderer_fill_caps (lines 16-18). The max_ver bound fetched at line 8 is never read, so no statement in this function ties the attacker-chosen version to the allocated size; a version whose caps layout exceeds or under-fills max_size yields a host-side heap overflow (or, because the buffer is g_malloc'd uninitialized and the full sizeof(*resp)+max_size is sent at line 19, disclosure of uninitialized host heap to the guest). Guest-to-host trust boundary crossing with memory-corruption impact.

op_format consumes only editor-internal operator/cursor state set up by the same-privilege local user's keystrokes; the snippet contains no memory, index, size, or injection sink fed by cross-boundary attacker data. The cursor-increment sink is correctly guarded by the quoted bound (curwin->w_cursor.lnum < curbuf->b_ml.ml_line_count), and the only arithmetic defect candidate (w_old_cursor_lnum/w_old_visual_lnum can become <= 0 after adding a negative line-count delta) has no consumer sink within the given code and no cross-privilege attacker, so its trigger consequence cannot be instantiated here. Callees u_save, format_lines, check_cursor, and the redraw consumers of w_old_* are not shown; their validation is an assumption, not evidence.

assumptions: u_save() (called with (linenr_T)(oap->start.lnum - 1) and (linenr_T)(oap->end.lnum + 1)) is assumed to validate its line-number arguments internally; its implementation is not in the given code, so no guard for that sink could be quoted.
format_lines(oap->line_count, keep_cursor) is assumed to operate safely on the buffer text it formats; it is not shown, and any vulnerability inside it cannot be analyzed here.
check_cursor() and beginline(BL_WHITE | BL_FIX) are assumed to repair invalid cursor positions after line deletion/joining; their implementations are not shown.

oap->start/end/cursor_start/line_count are assumed to originate from the editor's operator-pending state machine (normal.c) from the local user's own keystrokes, not from decoded external content; the setup code is not shown.

Downstream consumers of wp->w_old_cursor_lnum / wp->w_old_visual_lnum (redraw logic) are not shown and are assumed to tolerate non-positive values; no memory sink for those values exists in the given snippet.
limitations: wp->w_old_cursor_lnum += old_line_count (or w_old_visual_lnum) can produce 0 or a negative value when the line-count delta is negative with magnitude >= the stored line number (boundary: delta == -w_old_cursor_lnum yields exactly 0; larger magnitude yields negative). The guard 'if (wp->w_old_cursor_lnum != 0)' checks only the pre-value, and no post-value lower-bound check exists in this code. However, the result is consumed only by redraw bookkeeping not shown, the delta magnitude is bounded by lines the local user formatted, and the controlling party is the same-privilege editor user, so the trigger's security consequence could not be instantiated; recorded as a robustness/consistency defect, not a vulnerability.

curwin->w_cursor = oap->cursor_start and curwin->w_cursor = oap->start are performed without validation in this snippet; if the operator state machine ever stored an invalid position, later statements could use it. The producing statements are outside this code and on the same-privilege keystroke path, so this remains a contract question.
The asymmetry that w_old_visual_lnum is never adjusted when w_old_cursor_lnum == 0 can desynchronize Visual redraw hints; cosmetic effect only.
The analysis is limited to the shown function; vulnerabilities in u_save, format_lines, or the redraw code that consumes w_old_* would require those functions to be analyzed.

verdict.summary: bdrv_write_compressed performs NULL checks on drv and drv->bdrv_write_compressed, gates the request through bdrv_check_request on every path before both downstream uses (set_dirty_bitmap and the driver callback), and contains no memory, size, or injection sink of its own. All attacker-data (sector_num, nb_sectors) flows only into callees whose bodies are not shown, so no defective statement or instantiated trigger exists within this code; the behavior of bdrv_check_request and the driver's compressed-write callback is an unverifiable assumption, not a provable defect of this snippet.

assumptions: bdrv_check_request(bs, sector_num, nb_sectors) at line 9 is assumed to validate request bounds, sign of nb_sectors, image end, and arithmetic overflow; its body is not in the given code, so no enforcing bound can be quoted (GUARD ANCHORING).
drv->bdrv_write_compressed (qcow2 etc.) is assumed to handle the validated request safely; its body is not shown.
set_dirty_bitmap is assumed to size/index its bitmap consistently with the request range; its body is not shown.
bs is assumed non-NULL per interface contract; it is dereferenced at line 4 (bs->drv) without a check.
buf is assumed non-NULL and at least nb_sectors*512 bytes per interface contract; it is never dereferenced in this code.
limitations: C1: no explicit nb_sectors > 0 / sign check in this code before drv->bdrv_write_compressed (line 14); whether nb_sectors = 0 or negative is rejected depends entirely on the unshown bdrv_check_request, so the trigger could not be instantiated. If that callee accepts negative sizes, the defect would live there, not here.
C2/C3: potential int overflow of nb_sectors*512 (nb_sectors > 4194303) or int64 overflow of sector_num*512 — the multiplication is not performed by any statement in this code.
C4: potential out-of-bounds dirty-bitmap write in set_dirty_bitmap if the bitmap extent is smaller than sector_num+nb_sectors — sink is in an unshown callee; the only in-code gate is line 9.
C5: NULL or undersized buf is an interface-contract issue (contract branch), not attack data.
C6: TOCTOU on bs->drv (drv set to NULL concurrently with bdrv_close) — no two interleavable operations are exhibited in this code, and QEMU block-layer locking is external to this snippet.

Impact model: typical callers (qemu-img convert -c, block tooling) run at equal privilege with the party supplying the image; a crash confined to that process would be a robustness bug per discipline 3, further weakening any speculative trigger.

verdict.summary: This gRPC resolver-result handler consumes attacker-influenced resolver channel args (LB policy name, LB addresses, service config JSON) but every sink in the shown code is guarded by a quotable check: strcmp is preceded by 'if (lb_policy_name != NULL && ...)', the LB policy creation is preceded by 'if (lb_policy_name == NULL) lb_policy_name = "pick_first";' with a NULL-result check 'if (lb_policy != NULL)', the address loop is bounded by 'for (size_t i = 0; i < addresses->num_addresses; ++i)', and both lb_policy_name and service_config_json are duplicated via gpr_strdup before 'grpc_channel_args_destroy(exec_ctx, chand->resolver_result)' so no dangling pointers are used. Error refcounts (state_error) are balanced on all traced paths, and LB policy REF/UNREF pairs ('config_change', 'exit_idle', old policy swap) are balanced. Remaining candidates (NULL value.pointer.p dereference, state_error dangling if the callee never writes the out-param, assert crashes on mistyped args) all require a contract violation by the resolver component or a callee whose code is not shown, and none is producible by this code's own data flow; worst-case outcomes are process termination without memory corruption, disclosure, or amplification.

assumptions: grpc_lb_policy_check_connectivity(exec_ctx, lb_policy, &state_error) always assigns *state_error before returning; this code relies on that (it UNREFs state_error to zero refs immediately before the call) but the callee is not shown.

The resolver component (not shown) populates GRPC_ARG_LB_ADDRESSES with a non-NULL value.pointer.p whose addresses array is consistent with num_addresses; this code asserts only the arg type: 'GPR_ASSERT(channel_arg->type == GRPC_ARG_POINTER)'.
gpr_strdup's behavior on a NULL string argument (channel_arg->value.string could be NULL for GRPC_ARG_SERVICE_CONFIG / GRPC_ARG_LB_POLICY_NAME) is not shown.
grpc_service_config_create and method_parameters_create_from_json safely parse attacker-influenced JSON; the parsing implementation is not shown, so no defect can be attributed to it here.
The '_locked' suffix denotes that the channel combiner/channel mutex is held for all chand field accesses outside the info_mu critical section; the locking protocol is defined by code not shown.
limitations: NULL-pointer dereference candidate: if a resolver emitted GRPC_ARG_LB_ADDRESSES with type GRPC_ARG_POINTER and value.pointer.p == NULL, 'grpc_lb_addresses *addresses = channel_arg->value.pointer.p;' followed by 'for (size_t i = 0; i < addresses->num_addresses; ++i)' would crash; no NULL check exists in this code, but this code's own statements never produce that arg, so the trigger is a resolver contract violation (speculative).

Potential dangling state_error: 'GRPC_ERROR_UNREF(state_error)' drops the only reference and the pointer is only revalidated by the out-parameter of grpc_lb_policy_check_connectivity; a callee that can return without writing *error would leave a freed pointer that is later passed to GRPC_ERROR_REF. Callee behavior not shown; speculative.

GPR_ASSERT on channel-arg types ('GPR_ASSERT(channel_arg->type == GRPC_ARG_STRING)') aborts the process on a mistyped arg; only a misbehaving in-process resolver plugin can produce this, and the worst case is termination of the same-privilege process with no corruption or disclosure.

verdict.summary: hash_passwords replaces the intended per-password random salt with a constant 32-byte zero salt (std::memset(..., 0, 32)); the RAND_bytes call that would have generated it is present only as a commented-out block. Every password is therefore hashed with the identical, publicly predictable salt, so an attacker who later obtains the stored (salt, hash) pairs — the documented use is storage in a database — can precompute one lookup table effective against all users and all deployments, and identical passwords yield identical hashes, defeating the purpose of salting a KDF for credential storage.

evidence.reason: Every entry's salt is overwritten with 32 zero bytes immediately before it is used as the PBKDF2 salt, so all hashed passwords share a constant, predictable salt. Trigger fully instantiated on every execution (e.g., argv 'alice pw1' -> salt = 0x00*32 -> PBKDF2-SHA256('pw1', 0x00*32, 10000)); an attacker across the service boundary who reads the stored hash table can build a single precomputed dictionary for all users and deployments.

The salt-generation fix (RAND_bytes) exists in the source but is entirely commented out, so no executing statement on any path to the PKCS5_PBKDF2_HMAC salt parameter produces unpredictable salt material — the counterfactual patch test found no active guard.

The KDF consumes the constant zero salt from line 31 for every password, producing hashes that are identical for equal passwords and reproducible offline with a single precomputed table, defeating the credential-storage salting requirement.

assumptions: OpenSSL PKCS5_PBKDF2_HMAC and EVP_sha256 behave per their documented contracts; no defects assumed inside the library.
The output is stored/used beyond this process per the function's documented purpose ('for further storage in a database'), which is the trust boundary the salt exists to defend.
limitations: hash_passwords indexes passwords[i] for i < count without checking passwords.size() >= count; in this program main constructs std::vector<std::string> passwords(count) with the identical count, so out-of-bounds access would require a caller violating the documented parameter contract (contract argument, speculative here).

A negative 'count' would make std::vector<HashedPassword> hashed_passwords(count) convert the negative int to a huge size_t and throw/terminate, but main derives count as (argc-1)/2 from a non-negative argc, so this is unreachable in the given flow.
exit(1) on PBKDF2 failure is fail-terminate, not fail-open; no unvalidated data continues on that path.

verdict.summary: congratulate_user ignores the actual buffer capacity (buffer_size is never used) and passes snprintf a bound derived from the attacker-controlled username length: snprintf(buffer, 18 + userName_size + 1, ...) writes exactly 19 + strlen(username) bytes with no truncation. For a username of length >= 12 this exceeds the 30-byte stack buffer in main (19 + L > 30 when L > 11), producing an out-of-bounds stack write whose length and content are fully attacker-chosen.

evidence.reason: The snprintf bound is computed as 18 + userName_size + 1 (attacker-controlled length) instead of the actual buffer capacity; the parameter buffer_size (30 for the stack array in main) is never referenced in the body, so no guard bounds the write to the buffer. With userName_size = 12 the formatted output is 30 chars + NUL = 31 bytes written into the 30-byte stack buffer (one-past-limit), and longer usernames scale the overflow with attacker-chosen content — an out-of-bounds stack write (trigger fully instantiated in STEP 4).

Taint origin: strlen(argv[1]) passes the unbounded attacker-chosen length of argv[1] as userName_size, which line 15 converts directly into the snprintf write bound; nothing in this code caps it against the 30-byte buffer declared on line 27.

assumptions: argv strings are NUL-terminated per the C/POSIX contract, so strlen(argv[1]) is well-defined; this is an interface contract, not a defense.
This code is judged as the intake point for the username value; no bound on userName or userName_size is enforced by any statement in the given code (buffer_size is declared but never used).
limitations: Secondary speculative issue: 18 + userName_size + 1 can overflow signed int if userName_size is near INT_MAX (UB, possibly a negative snprintf size), but triggering it requires a ~2 GB argument and no statement in this code produces such a value in the shown entrypoint; not the driver of the verdict.

In the shown entrypoint the username arrives via argv from the user who launched the process; the memory-corruption write is nonetheless a genuine out-of-bounds write on attacker-controlled data crossing into the function as a public data-carrying parameter, and the same function called with any externally sourced username (e.g., from a service) is directly exploitable.

verdict.summary: No security vulnerability found. The hashing loop's index bound is enforced inside the given code by pairing 'int count = (argc - 1) / 2;' and 'std::vector<std::string> passwords(count);' with the loop 'for (int i = 0; i < count; i++)', so passwords[i] is in bounds on every executed path. The KDF uses RAND_bytes (CSPRNG) for a fresh 32-byte salt per password and PKCS5_PBKDF2_HMAC with SHA-256 and 10000 iterations exactly as its documented contract specifies, with output buffer size hash.size()==32 matching the request. Error paths fail closed (exit(1)). The only hypothetical defect, an out-of-bounds read if a caller passed count larger than the vector sizes, requires an invisible external caller violating the documented parameter contract and cannot be instantiated by any path in this code; worst case for the visible CLI is a crash of the invoker's own equal-privilege process. The 10000-iteration count is below modern OWASP guidance but is the value the specification mandates, so it is recorded as a hardening note, not a defect.

assumptions: argv[0..argc-1] are valid NUL-terminated strings and argv[argc] is NULL, per the C/C++ standard main contract; the code's own index arithmetic (2 + 2*i <= argc-1 for i < count) never reaches the NULL sentinel because 'if (argc < 3) ... return 1;' rejects undersized argv and count = (argc-1)/2 pairs the arguments.
RAND_bytes and PKCS5_PBKDF2_HMAC follow their documented OpenSSL contracts (return 1 on success); the code checks those return values and fails closed.
limitations: Contract-based out-of-bounds candidate (not a vulnerability here): if an external caller invoked hash_passwords(count, usernames, passwords) with count greater than passwords.size()/usernames.size(), 'for (int i = 0; i < count; i++)' would index passwords[i] out of bounds. No such caller exists in this code; main constructs 'std::vector<std::string> passwords(count);' and 'std::vector<std::string> usernames(count);' so every executed path is in bounds, and the documented parameter contract ties count to the list sizes. A defensive size check would be hardening, not a fix for a reachable defect.

The 10000 PBKDF2 iteration count is below current OWASP recommendations (~600k for PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256), but the problem statement explicitly mandates 10000 iterations, 32-byte salt, and SHA-256, and the code implements exactly that; recorded as a hardening/spec observation (CWE-330/CWE-327 do not apply: RAND_bytes is a CSPRNG, the salt is fresh and full-length, and the primitive is not broken).

exit(1) on RAND_bytes or PKCS5_PBKDF2_HMAC failure terminates the process; these failures require OS/entropy/allocation conditions an attacker cannot induce, and the paths fail closed, so they are robustness behavior rather than denial-of-service vulnerabilities.

The usernames parameter is accepted and filled but never used by hash_passwords; with no visible caller other than main, argv-derived worst cases (odd argument count dropping the last unpaired argument) affect only the equal-privilege user invoking the tool on their own arguments.

verdict.summary: bdrv_write_compressed validates driver presence (lines 5, 7) and routes sector_num/nb_sectors through bdrv_check_request (line 9) on the only path to the sinks (set_dirty_bitmap, line 12; driver dispatch, line 14), performing no arithmetic on attacker-influenced values itself. Any out-of-bounds consequence would require the not-shown helper bdrv_check_request to accept out-of-range inputs (e.g., sector_num < 0, nb_sectors <= 0, or sector_num + nb_sectors overflow) together with a caller supplying such values — a trigger that cannot be instantiated from statements in this code, and whose worst case at this entry point is confined to the equal-privilege operator's own process. No guard on the parameters is quotable from the given code, so this is recorded as an assumption, not as proof of safety.

assumptions: The implementation of bdrv_check_request (called at line 9) is not part of the given code; per guard anchoring it cannot be quoted, so the assumption that it rejects sector_num < 0, nb_sectors <= 0, and sector_num + nb_sectors beyond device bounds is unverifiable from this code. This candidate defect in the helper is recorded rather than used to either prove safety or confirm a vulnerability in this code.
bs is assumed non-NULL per the BlockDriverState interface contract; line 4 (BlockDriverState dereference 'bs->drv') has no local NULL check.
The callee driver's bdrv_write_compressed implementation (line 14) and set_dirty_bitmap (line 12) are not shown; their internal bounds behavior is outside the given code.
limitations: Speculative candidate (contract): caller passing bs == NULL causes a NULL-pointer dereference at line 4 ('BlockDriver *drv = bs->drv;'). Requires a caller violating the documented non-NULL contract; no statement in this code produces a NULL bs. Robustness/contract issue, not a vulnerability here.

Speculative candidate (uninstantiated trigger): attacker-influenced sector_num/nb_sectors (e.g., sector_num = -1, nb_sectors = -1, or sector_num near INT64_MAX causing wrap) reaching set_dirty_bitmap (line 12) or the driver dispatch (line 14) unvalidated. The only guard is 'if (bdrv_check_request(bs, sector_num, nb_sectors)) return -EIO;' at line 9, whose body is not shown; triggering the harm requires the unshown helper to accept out-of-range values, which no statement in this code exhibits, and the code performs no arithmetic that could itself produce a bad value. Additionally, callers of this API supply equal-privilege arguments, so the worst instantiated outcome is a crash of the operator's own process.

Logic nit: set_dirty_bitmap (line 12) marks sectors dirty before the driver write at line 14 executes and regardless of its result; this is a dirty-bitmap consistency issue with no memory-safety or cross-boundary security consequence.
nb_sectors == 0 (degenerate request) is passed through unvalidated; its behavior depends entirely on the not-shown callee.

verdict.summary: All buffer accesses are provably in bounds: the fixed indices b[367] and b[i..i+7] (i < 496, max index 502) stay inside ut8 b[512], the buffer is pre-zeroed with ZERO_FILL so short reads cannot expose uninitialized stack data, the read-length argument matches the destination size (512), and the scan loop is a fixed-cost constant bound. The only unguarded dereference (entry from r_bin_pe_get_entrypoint is never NULL-checked before entry->paddr is used) requires the external callee to violate its contract or an allocation failure to trigger, and its worst case is a crash of the same process that opened the attacker's file, so it is recorded as a limitation, not a vulnerability in this code.

assumptions: follow_offset(entry, pe->b, b, sizeof(b), big_endian, offset) is a helper not shown in the given code; its internal bounds handling cannot be quoted here, so its safety is unverifiable from this code alone. The offsets passed (367 and i+7 with i <= 495, so at most 502) leave at least 10 bytes of headroom in the 512-byte buffer, but this is arithmetic, not a verified guard.
r_bin_pe_get_entrypoint is assumed to return a non-NULL allocated struct on success; it is an external callee whose failure modes are not shown. This code does not itself produce a NULL entry.
limitations: entry is not NULL-checked before entry->paddr is dereferenced in the r_buf_read_at call and the pe_printf argument; if r_bin_pe_get_entrypoint ever returned NULL (allocation failure or internal error not visible in this code), this function would dereference NULL and crash the analysis process. Trigger is speculative (requires callee contract violation or OOM) and the impact is confined to the process of the party that opened the file, so it is a robustness issue rather than a security vulnerability in this code.

r_buf_read_at may perform a partial read (return value between 1 and 511 is accepted by the '< 1' check); this is safe here only because ZERO_FILL(b) precedes the read, so the unread tail reads as zeros rather than as uninitialized stack memory.

verdict.summary: The function performs scalar timestamp rescaling with no memory indexing, allocation, copy, or injection sinks. The only in-code guards that exist ('if (den && num)' before the duration rescale and 'frame_size >= 0' before av_frac_add) were quoted and hold on all paths; the 64-bit products of 32-bit operands cannot overflow. The remaining candidates (divisor AV_TIME_BASE*st->time_base.num becoming 0, possible uninitialized num/den, av_rescale edge behavior on INT64_MIN) all have their defective statement inside callees not shown, whose behavior cannot be verified from this code, so they are recorded as speculative.

assumptions: av_rescale's behavior for zero/negative divisor and for extreme int64 inputs is not shown; no claim about it is used to confirm or dismiss a finding.
compute_frame_duration's write behavior for *num/*den is not shown; the code assumes it always writes them, else 'if (den && num)' would read uninitialized values (CWE-457).
get_audio_frame_size and av_frac_add implementations are not shown; their use here is guarded by 'frame_size >= 0' for the in-code decision only.
It is assumed st and pkt are non-NULL and st->time_base is set by the demuxer; these are interface-contract conditions, not attack data.
Whether any calling demuxer can leave st->time_base.num == 0 at this call site cannot be established from this code.
limitations: Speculative: if st->time_base.num == 0 (parsed stream header field), AV_TIME_BASE * (int64_t)st->time_base.num == 0 is passed as the divisor to av_rescale on the pts, dts, and duration rescales with no guard in this code ('av_rescale(pkt->pts, st->time_base.den, AV_TIME_BASE * (int64_t)st->time_base.num)'). A divide-by-zero crash would occur only inside av_rescale, which is not shown, so the trigger cannot be fully instantiated here.

Speculative: 'int num, den;' are uninitialized locals; if compute_frame_duration (not shown) has a path that returns without writing them, 'if (den && num)' reads indeterminate values. Callee-contract dependent.

Crash-type effects (SIGFPE/abort) inside the not-shown av_rescale on malformed stream headers would be a denial of service in a demuxer processing untrusted media files, but confirming it requires the callee's code.
Timestamp-logic quirks (negative last_IP_pts handling, pts/dts heuristics) affect output timestamps only; no memory, authz, or amplification consequence was identified.

verdict.summary: extract_tar_to_path extracts attacker-controlled tar archives with no effective path confinement: the only guard, is_path_safe(), is a stub that unconditionally returns true, so entry pathnames containing '../' traversals, absolute paths, or symlink components are concatenated with dest_path and passed to archive_write_header, allowing arbitrary file write/overwrite outside the destination directory with attacker-chosen content and permissions.

evidence.reason: Sink: the attacker-controlled tar entry pathname (current_file = archive_entry_pathname(entry)) is concatenated with dest_path and written to disk via archive_write_header with no traversal filtering; flags (ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_TIME | ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_PERM) include no secure-symlink/dotdot options. An entry named e.g. '../../tmp/evil.sh' instantiates a write outside the destination directory.

Origin of the missing check: the sole path-validation guard invoked at line 117 ('if (!is_path_safe(current_file))') unconditionally returns true, so every traversal/absolute/symlink pathname passes the first-pass validation, leaving the extraction path fully attacker-controlled.

assumptions: libarchive's archive_write_data_block is assumed to validate block size/offset consistency internally against the entry's declared size; that library-internal enforcement is not quotable in this code and was not relied on for the primary finding.
The tar file contents are treated as attacker data (originator of untrusted data), consistent with the function's role as the decoder and extraction point.
limitations: Speculative: archive_entry_pathname returning NULL for a malformed header would make snprintf receive a NULL %s argument (UB/crash); this requires the libarchive contract to be violated and is a robustness issue, not an instantiated security impact.
PATH_MAX 512 truncation of very long entry names in snprintf is a correctness quirk with no distinct security consequence identified.
CWE-59 symlink-following extraction is a variant of the same missing-confinement root cause and is subsumed by the CWE-22 finding.

verdict.summary: The only memory-safety sink, the allocation-size computation n*lb, is fully guarded by the textbook overflow check `if (lb && n > GC_SIZE_MAX / lb) return NULL;`, which lies on every path ahead of both uses, leaves n and lb unmutated, and holds at all boundary values (lb=0, n=0, n=GC_SIZE_MAX with lb=1, exact-quotient and one-past-quotient cases). No injection, path, crypto, or authz sinks exist in this code. The notable residual concern is that this calloc wrapper never clears the returned memory, relying entirely on the not-shown REDIRECT_MALLOC / GC_malloc_uncollectable to satisfy calloc's zeroing contract; that behavior cannot be verified from the given code, so it is recorded as a limitation rather than a confirmed finding.

assumptions: GC_SIZE_MAX is assumed equal to the width-max of size_t (SIZE_MAX); the guard's correctness for unsigned wrap depends on this compile-time constant, which is not defined in the given code.
REDIRECT_MALLOC and GC_malloc_uncollectable are assumed to be allocation functions accepting a byte count and permitted to return NULL or a minimal object for size 0; their definitions are not shown.

GC_libpthread_start/End and GC_libld_start/End are assumed zero-initialized globals set by GC_init_lib_bounds(); their declarations are not shown. With zero bounds the caller-range test fails closed (caller >= 0 && caller < 0 is false).
limitations: Missing zero-clear (potential CWE-665/CWE-908 information disclosure): this calloc replacement never clears the returned block, and in the Boehm-Demers-Weiser collector's typical -DREDIRECT_MALLOC=GC_malloc configuration the callee does not clear either, which would violate calloc's documented zeroing contract and disclose stale heap contents to any caller. Because REDIRECT_MALLOC's semantics are outside the given code, the trigger precondition (callee returns uncleared memory) could not be instantiated from the given code; a one-line fix (memset the block before returning, or route through a zeroing allocator) is absent from this function.

Benign race on `static GC_bool lib_bounds_set`: two threads may each execute GC_init_lib_bounds() before either sets the flag; the in-code comment asserts no memory-visibility guarantee is needed. No harmful interleaved state is exhibited by statements in this code.

The return value of GC_init_lib_bounds() is unchecked; if it fails to set the library bounds the subsequent range test falls through safely to the normal allocator, at worst changing allocation policy (collectable vs uncollectable), with no attacker-influencable input involved.

Allocation failure of REDIRECT_MALLOC(n*lb) for huge (but non-wrapping) products such as n*lb == GC_SIZE_MAX results in a NULL or failed allocation; this is environment/allocator failure no attacker input can turn into memory corruption within this code.

verdict.summary: The hostname validation of the attacker-supplied 'logout' redirect target is gated on 'uri.hostname != NULL', so any URL that parses successfully but carries no host component (e.g. 'javascript:alert(1)', 'data:text/html,...', 'http:/evil.com') skips host validation entirely and is used as the post-logout redirect target. Additionally, the check anchors on the Host-header-derived current host (line 38), which the same network peer controls. The unvalidated URL flows to oidc_handle_logout_request() as the redirect destination, enabling open redirect/phishing and script execution via javascript:/data: schemes.

evidence.reason: The hostname check is short-circuited when uri.hostname is NULL, so a successfully parsed hostname-less URL such as 'javascript:alert(1)' bypasses all host validation (verified: apr_uri_parse at line 28 succeeds with hostname NULL, this condition evaluates false, and only the CRLF check at lines 57-58 still applies) and reaches the redirect sink 'oidc_handle_logout_request(r, c, session, url)'. Moreover c_host originates from the attacker-controlled Host header (line 38), so even hostname-bearing foreign URLs can pass. No statement in this function rejects a hostname-less or Host-matching foreign logout URL — the counterfactual guard is genuinely absent.

Origin of the tainted redirect target: the 'logout' request parameter is read from the HTTP request, i.e. content fully controlled by an unauthenticated network peer, and flows into the validation bypass at lines 39-41 and the redirect sink at the function's final oidc_handle_logout_request() call.

assumptions: oidc_is_front_channel_logout/oidc_is_back_channel_logout and oidc_handle_logout_request are not shown; it is assumed the former recognize only the module's own logout endpoint forms and the latter issues a redirect to 'url' (per the post_logout_redirect_uri semantics and the in-function comment 'validate the URL' and 'prevent HTTP header splitting'), which is the documented behavior of this module's logout flow.
apr_uri_parse (APR) parses 'javascript:alert(1)' successfully with uri.hostname == NULL, which is APR's documented behavior for scheme-only/relative URLs.
limitations: If oidc_get_current_url_host(r) (line 38) can return NULL (e.g., missing Host header), strstr(c_host, ...) would dereference NULL and crash the worker; the NULL producer is not in this listing, so this crash path is speculative and was not counted as a finding.
The CRLF check (lines 57-58) and the escaping of url in the post_logout_redirect_uri psprintf guard against HTTP header splitting; no injection finding is claimed there.
oidc_debug(r, "enter (url=%s)", url) uses a constant format string, so no format-string finding.

verdict.summary: Static internal table-initialization helper; all parameters (elemsize, inc, y_tab) are internal contract values from the same conversion module, not attacker-originated data. The only in-code sink (table[i] write) is guarded by 'for (i = 0; i < 256 + 2*YUVRGB_TABLE_HEADROOM; i++)' matching the array extent exactly. Pointer-arithmetic candidates against the y_tab allocation require a caller-contract violation (inc/allocation mismatch) that no statement in this code can produce.

assumptions: YUVRGB_TABLE_HEADROOM is a compile-time constant consistent between the array declaration in the signature and the loop bound.

The caller (swscale table init, not shown) allocates y_tab consistently with inc and elemsize per its documented internal contract; this is a contract assumption, not a guard relied on for any dismissed candidate whose data reaches a sink here.
limitations: Speculative: if a caller passed an inc/elemsize/allocation-size combination inconsistent with the internal table layout, the unchecked pointer arithmetic 'y_table + elemsize * (cb >> 16)' and the pre-loop 'y_table -= elemsize * (inc >> 9)' could write pointers referencing out-of-allocation memory; no such caller is in this code and the values are internal configuration, not attacker data.
